title: A balanced diet: different plates for different people, and what a missing nutrient does

summary.text: A child can eat until she is full every day and still fall ill, because one nutrient is missing. How can a tiny amount matter so much? In this unit you will time how long your eyes take to see in a dim room, and boil cabbage to see where the vitamin C goes.
summary.art: A steel plate of rice, dal and greens beside a tiny speck of chalk dust on a dark cloth, with a magnifying glass over the speck.

intro.hook: The iodine your body needs in a whole day is a tiny amount. It weighs about the same as a speck of chalk dust the size of a full stop. Why would a body fall ill for want of something so small?
intro.text: Most people think a good diet means enough food. Enough food stops hunger, but it does not always stop illness. Sailors with full stomachs lost their teeth, because their food had no vitamin C. Families who ate plenty of white rice lost the strength in their legs. The polished rice had lost its vitamin B1. These are called deficiency diseases. In this unit you weigh out one day's needs, starting with two spoons of protein, which is a lot, and ending with a tiny amount of iodine. To see how tiny, you will put a speck of chalk dust beside it, because the two weigh about the same. You time your own eyes in a dark room. You test what boiling does to the vitamin C in cabbage. You also find out why your plate should not look like your grandmother's plate.
intro.art: A child's hand placing a speck of chalk dust beside a heap of sugar on a dark steel plate.

outcomes: I can say what a balanced diet is: enough of every nutrient, with water and fibre, for one person's body.
I can match each deficiency disease to its missing nutrient, and name a cheap food that prevents it.
I can explain why nutrients needed in tiny amounts still matter, and what hidden hunger is.
I can explain, with numbers, why a baby, a pregnant woman, a worker and an old person need different diets.
I can give four ways to make cheap food more nourishing, and say why each one works.
I can explain how fortified food, sunlight and tablets prevent deficiency, and why too much can harm.
I can run a fair test with food or with my own eyes, and say what the result shows.
I can tell how doctors found the cause of goitre, and say what is still unsure about kwashiorkor.

terms.meaning: A substance in food that the body needs to work, grow and stay healthy. Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals are nutrients.
terms.example: Dal gives the nutrient protein. A guava gives the nutrient vitamin C.
terms.art: Five small bowls in a row holding rice, dal, oil, a guava and a pinch of salt.

terms.meaning: Food and drink that give one person enough of every nutrient, water and fibre, and not too much of any.
terms.example: Ragi dosa with sambar, a greens poriyal, curd and a guava make a balanced meal for a child.
terms.art: A steel plate with a cereal, a pulse, a green vegetable, curd and a fruit, each in its own part.

terms.meaning: An illness caused by too little of one nutrient over a long time. Deficiency means not having enough.
terms.example: Scurvy is a deficiency disease. It comes from too little vitamin C.
terms.art: An outline of a body with one small empty gap shaped like a jigsaw piece.

terms.meaning: A substance that the body needs in very small amounts and cannot make enough of. It must come from food. Vitamin D is the exception, because skin makes it in sunlight.
terms.example: Humans cannot make vitamin C, so we must eat it. A goat makes her own.
terms.art: A lemon, a carrot, an egg and a sun, each with a letter beside it: C, A, B and D.

terms.meaning: A nutrient that first came from rocks, soil or sea water. Plants take minerals up through their roots.
terms.example: Iron, iodine and calcium are minerals.
terms.art: A plant root in soil with tiny dots moving from the soil into the root.

terms.meaning: A nutrient needed in tiny amounts, measured in milligrams or micrograms. Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients.
terms.example: A child needs about 30 grams of protein a day, but only about 100 micrograms of iodine. That is a very small amount.
terms.art: A kitchen spoon heaped with sugar beside a speck of chalk dust.

terms.meaning: One millionth of a gram. One thousand micrograms make one milligram, and one thousand milligrams make one gram.
terms.example: A speck of chalk dust the size of a full stop weighs very roughly 100 micrograms. Specks differ in size, so this is only a rough figure. We use a speck here only because it is small and easy to picture.
terms.art: One grain of salt on a fingertip, drawn very large.

terms.meaning: Being short of a vitamin or a mineral while eating enough food to feel full.
terms.example: A child who eats mostly white rice and biscuits may feel full and still be short of iron.
terms.art: A child with a full plate of plain white rice, and a faint outline of missing vegetables beside it.

terms.meaning: Poor health from the wrong amount of food or of a nutrient for a long time. It can be too little or too much.
terms.example: Too little iron is malnutrition. So is far too much sugar and fat.
terms.art: A see-saw with a nearly empty plate at one end and a plate piled with sweets and chips at the other.

terms.meaning: Having too little haemoglobin in the blood, so the body gets less oxygen. The person feels tired and breathless and looks pale. Too little iron is the most common cause.
terms.example: A girl with anaemia may be out of breath after one flight of stairs.
terms.art: A tired girl resting on a staircase, with a small circle showing pale red blood cells.

terms.meaning: The red substance inside red blood cells that carries oxygen. Each haemoglobin molecule holds four atoms of iron.
terms.example: A health worker pricks a finger and measures the haemoglobin in one drop of blood.
terms.art: A red blood cell drawn large, with tiny dots of iron inside it and small circles of oxygen holding on.

terms.meaning: Not being able to see in dim light, although sight is normal in bright light. It is the first sign of too little vitamin A.
terms.example: A child with night blindness trips over the doorstep at dusk.
terms.art: A child at a doorway at dusk reaching out with her hands, while another child walks past easily.

terms.meaning: An orange substance that plants make. The human body turns carotene into vitamin A.
terms.example: Carrot, papaya, pumpkin and drumstick leaves are rich in carotene.
terms.art: A carrot, a slice of papaya and a sprig of drumstick leaves with an arrow pointing to an eye.

terms.meaning: A disease in which a child's bones stay soft and the legs bend. It comes from too little vitamin D, and often too little calcium.
terms.example: A toddler with rickets may have legs that bow outwards.
terms.art: A toddler standing in sunlight with slightly bowed legs, and the leg bones shown as curved lines.

terms.meaning: A swelling at the front of the neck. The thyroid gland grows bigger there, usually because the food has too little iodine.
terms.example: Goitre was once common in the Himalayas, where the soil has little iodine.
terms.art: A side view of a neck with a butterfly-shaped gland drawn at the front, shown at normal size and enlarged.

terms.meaning: A disease in which the gums bleed, teeth loosen and wounds do not heal. It comes from too little vitamin C.
terms.example: Sailors on long voyages got scurvy when they had no fresh fruit or vegetables.
terms.art: An old sailing ship with a barrel of lemons on the deck.

terms.meaning: A disease in which the legs become weak and numb and the heart grows weak. It comes from too little vitamin B1.
terms.example: Beriberi spread when people began to eat rice polished white by machines.
terms.art: A bowl of white polished rice beside a bowl of brown unpolished rice, with a heap of bran between them.

terms.meaning: A serious kind of malnutrition in young children. The feet, legs and face swell with water, and the skin and hair change.
terms.example: Kwashiorkor often begins after a child stops breastfeeding and eats mostly thin, starchy porridge.
terms.art: A doctor gently pressing a thumb on a small child's swollen foot, leaving a dent.

terms.meaning: A serious kind of malnutrition from too little food of every kind. The child becomes very thin, with no swelling.
terms.example: In a famine, when there is little of any food, many children get marasmus.
terms.art: A health worker measuring the thin upper arm of a small child with a coloured tape.

terms.meaning: Food with a nutrient added on purpose, so that everyone who eats it gets enough.
terms.example: Iodised salt is salt fortified with iodine.
terms.art: A packet of salt with the word 'iodised' on it, and a packet of oil marked with a small +F sign.

terms.meaning: The part of plant food that human enzymes cannot digest. It holds water and keeps food moving through the gut.
terms.example: Whole wheat atta, ragi, rajma, guava and greens are rich in fibre.
terms.art: A sieve holding brown flakes of bran over a heap of fine white flour.

explanations.definition: A balanced diet gives one person enough of every nutrient, water and fibre, and not too much of any.
explanations.description: The body needs seven things from food and drink. Carbohydrates and fats give energy. Proteins build and repair the body. Vitamins and minerals keep its chemistry working. Water carries everything, and makes up more than half of your weight. Fibre keeps food moving through the gut. No single food holds all seven in the right amounts, so a balanced diet needs variety. Balance has two sides. A diet can be unbalanced because something is missing. It can also be unbalanced because there is too much sugar, salt or fat. The words 'for one person' matter too. A plate that suits a woman who works at a desk is too small for a fast-growing girl.
examples: Rice alone gives energy, but little protein and almost no vitamin A or vitamin C.
Rice with sambar, a greens poriyal and curd covers energy, protein, iron, calcium and several vitamins.
The same full plate every day, with two packets of chips added, is unbalanced the other way.
explanations.art: A steel plate divided into parts for a cereal, a pulse, vegetables, curd and fruit, with a tumbler of water beside it.

explanations.concept: Grams, milligrams and micrograms: why tiny amounts matter
explanations.definition: Macronutrients are needed in grams each day. Micronutrients are needed in milligrams or micrograms. A lack of either causes illness.
explanations.description: A child of ten needs about 30 grams of protein a day. That is about two heaped tablespoons. The same child needs about 50 milligrams of vitamin C. One moong seed weighs about 50 milligrams, so that is the weight of vitamin C a child needs in a day. The child also needs about 100 micrograms of iodine. A speck of chalk dust the size of a full stop weighs very roughly 100 micrograms, so that is about the weight of iodine a child needs in a day. The seed and the chalk dust do not contain these nutrients here. We use them only to show how little each nutrient weighs. The amounts are very different because the nutrients do different jobs. Protein is building material, so the body needs a lot of it. Iodine is a tiny part of a messenger substance called thyroid hormone. Each messenger needs only a few atoms of iodine. But the body cannot make the messenger without those atoms. A person can eat enough to feel full and still be short of a micronutrient. This is called hidden hunger. It is hidden because fullness tells the body about energy and bulk. No feeling tells you that iodine or vitamin A is running low.
examples: One grain of table salt weighs roughly 60 micrograms, and grains differ in size.
A child needs only about 2 micrograms of vitamin B12 in a day. That weighs about one thirtieth of a single grain of table salt. We compare it to salt only to show how tiny the amount is.
India's health survey of 2019 to 2021 found anaemia in more than half of the women tested.
explanations.art: A dark plate with four heaps in a row, from a spoonful of sugar down to a speck of chalk dust, each with a label.

explanations.concept: Vitamins: what goes wrong when one is missing
explanations.definition: A vitamin is a substance that the body needs in small amounts and cannot make enough of. Each vitamin does its own job, so each lack causes its own disease.
explanations.description: Vitamin A builds the substance in the eye that catches dim light. Without it, a person cannot see at dusk. This is night blindness. If the lack goes on, the surface of the eye dries, and the child can go blind. Vitamin B1 helps cells get energy out of starch and sugar. Without it, nerves and the heart weaken. This is beriberi. Vitamin C helps build collagen, the strong threads in skin, gums and blood vessels. Without it, gums bleed and wounds stay open. This is scurvy. Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium. Without it, a child's bones stay soft and bend. This is rickets. Most animals make their own vitamin C. Humans, other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs and fruit bats cannot, because one gene needed for it no longer works. Vitamin B12 is made only by bacteria. Plants hold almost none, so people who eat no meat or fish get theirs from milk, curd and eggs.
examples: A child short of vitamin A sees well at noon but stumbles in a dim room.
In 1747 the ship's doctor James Lind gave two sailors with scurvy oranges and lemons. They recovered fastest. One was fit for duty again in six days.
A baby kept indoors all winter can get rickets, even with enough milk.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: an eye at dusk, a leg with wavy nerve lines, a mouth with red gums, and a bent leg bone.

explanations.definition: Minerals are nutrients that first came from rock, soil and sea. Iron carries oxygen in the blood, iodine makes thyroid hormone, and calcium hardens bones and teeth.
explanations.description: Iron sits inside haemoglobin, the red substance that carries oxygen in the blood. With too little iron, the body makes too little haemoglobin. Less oxygen reaches the muscles and the brain. The person is tired, breathless and pale. This is anaemia, and it is the most common deficiency in India. The body absorbs iron from meat and fish easily. It absorbs iron from plants less easily. Vitamin C in the same meal helps, and tea or coffee with the meal hinders. Iodine is needed by the thyroid, a gland at the front of the neck. The thyroid makes a hormone that sets how fast every cell uses energy. With too little iodine, the gland grows larger to catch more, and the neck swells. This is goitre. If a pregnant woman is short of iodine, her baby's brain may not grow fully. Calcium makes bones and teeth hard, and nerves and muscles use it too. A growing child lays down new bone every day.
examples: Ragi has about three times as much calcium as the same weight of milk.
A squeeze of lemon on kala chana helps the gut absorb more of the iron.
Before iodised salt, goitre was common in the hills from Kashmir to Nagaland.
explanations.art: A red blood cell, a butterfly-shaped gland on a neck and a leg bone, each joined by a line to a food: kala chana, a salt packet and a ragi ball.

explanations.concept: Protein, energy and the most serious malnutrition
explanations.definition: A young child may get far too little food, or food that is almost all starch. Then growth stops, and the body breaks down its own muscle. The two severe forms are marasmus and kwashiorkor.
explanations.description: In marasmus the child gets too little of everything. The body burns its fat and then its muscle for energy. The child becomes very thin, and the skin hangs loose. In kwashiorkor the child may get some energy, often from thin maize or rice porridge. The feet, legs and face swell with water. The skin peels and the hair turns thin and pale. The swelling can hide how thin the child is. Both happen mostly between six months and five years of age. At that age a child grows fast, has a small stomach and catches many infections. Health workers find children at risk with a simple tape around the upper arm. Treatment is slow, careful feeding with special foods at a health centre. Prevention starts with breast milk alone for the first six months. After that come soft family foods with dal, egg, milk, oil and vegetables, several times a day.
examples: Anganwadi workers weigh young children every month and mark the weight on a growth chart.
A tape that shows red around a small child's upper arm means the child needs help at once.
After a long bout of loose motions, a small child needs extra food for two weeks to catch up.
explanations.art: An anganwadi worker reading a hanging weighing scale with a small child in a cloth sling, and a growth chart on the wall.

explanations.concept: Why your eyes need vitamin A
explanations.definition: The cells that see in dim light hold a light-catching substance called rhodopsin. The eye builds rhodopsin from vitamin A and a protein.
explanations.description: At the back of the eye is a thin layer called the retina. It holds two kinds of light-catching cells. Cones work in bright light and see colour. Rods work in dim light and see only light and dark. Each rod is packed with rhodopsin. When light strikes a rhodopsin molecule, the molecule changes shape and comes apart. That change starts the signal to the brain. Bright light breaks rhodopsin faster than the eye can rebuild it. So when you walk from sunlight into a dark room, your rods have almost none, and you see nothing. Over the next 20 to 30 minutes the eye rebuilds its rhodopsin, and dim things appear one by one. This is called dark adaptation. The eye needs a steady supply of vitamin A for the rebuilding. A person short of vitamin A rebuilds too little. Their eyes stay nearly blind in dim light, however long they wait.
examples: In the Dark Room Test, a white towel shows up within a minute, but a dark book takes several minutes.
A torch shone in your eyes at night leaves you blind to the dark for minutes afterwards.
Vitamin A drops are given to young children in India twice a year to protect their eyes.
explanations.art: A side view of an eye with the back layer drawn large, showing thin rod cells and fatter cone cells.

explanations.definition: How much of each nutrient a person needs depends on four things. They are body size, growth, how hard the muscles work, and whether the person is feeding another body.
explanations.description: Growth needs building material. A baby doubles their birth weight in about five months. So for each kilogram they need far more food than a grown-up. A child of two needs about 85 kilocalories for each kilogram of body weight. A woman who works at a desk needs about 30. A kilocalorie is the unit for the energy in food. Girls and boys from 10 to 18 grow fast. They need more protein, calcium and iron than at any time since babyhood. Girls need extra iron, because they will soon lose some blood every month. A pregnant woman builds a whole new body, so she needs more energy, protein, iron, folate and iodine. A breastfeeding mother makes about 750 millilitres of milk a day, which costs her about 600 kilocalories. A person who does heavy work with their muscles needs much more energy and water. An old person needs less energy, but just as much protein and more calcium. Their food should be soft to chew. A sick person needs fluids first, and extra food while they recover.
examples: A woman who carries loads all day needs about 1,000 kilocalories more than a woman at a desk.
A two-year-old has a small stomach, so they need five or six small meals a day.
Pregnant women in India are given iron and folic acid tablets at the health centre.
explanations.art: Six different plates in a row, each a different size and with different foods, with a small figure beside each: a toddler, a girl, a teenage girl, a pregnant woman, a worker and a grandmother.

explanations.concept: Cheap ways to make food more nourishing
explanations.definition: Some of the most nourishing foods are among the cheapest. The way food is paired, prepared and cooked also changes how much nourishment the body gets.
explanations.description: Pair a cereal with a pulse. Proteins are built from 20 kinds of units called amino acids. The body cannot make nine of them. Rice and wheat are low in one, called lysine. Dals are low in another, called methionine. Eaten together, each fills the other's gap. Sprout whole pulses. A dry moong seed has almost no vitamin C, and a sprouted one makes their own. Ferment batters. The bacteria and yeasts in idli batter make some B vitamins as they grow. Choose millets and greens. Ragi is rich in calcium, bajra in iron, and drumstick leaves in carotene, iron and calcium. Cook to keep vitamins. Vitamin C and the B vitamins dissolve in water. So wash vegetables before cutting, cook them in little water with a lid, and use the cooking water. Help the iron along. Add lemon or tomato to iron foods, and keep tea away from meals. Food cooked in an iron kadai also picks up some iron.
examples: Idli, pongal, khichdi, rajma with rice and dal with roti all pair a cereal with a pulse.
In the Cooking Water Test, the water from boiled cabbage cleared the blue liquid in fewer spoons than plain water.
A handful of roasted chana and groundnuts costs less than a packet of chips and gives far more protein.
explanations.art: A kitchen counter with soaked moong sprouting in a cloth, a pot of risen idli batter, a bunch of drumstick leaves and a black iron kadai.

explanations.concept: Preventing deficiency: food, fortified food, sunlight and tablets
explanations.definition: Deficiency is prevented in four ways. They are a varied diet, nutrients added to common foods, sunlight on skin, and tablets or drops from health workers.
explanations.description: Varied food comes first, because whole foods carry many nutrients together. But some soils hold little iodine, so no local food can supply it. So iodine is added to salt, which nearly everyone eats in nearly the same small amount. This is called fortification. In India some oil and milk are fortified with vitamins A and D, and some atta and rice with iron. Fortified packets carry a small +F sign. Vitamin D is different. Skin makes it when strong sunlight falls on it. The Sun must be high in the sky, and window glass blocks the rays that do this. Some people need more than food can easily give. Young children in India get vitamin A drops twice a year. Schoolchildren and pregnant women get iron and folic acid tablets. These are given in measured doses, because more is not better. Too much vitamin A or iron is a poison. So vitamin and iron tablets are taken only on the advice of a doctor or a health worker.
examples: Iodised salt in India must hold at least 15 micrograms of iodine in each gram when you buy it.
In the Short Shadow Test, the pencil's shadow was shorter than the pencil only around the middle of the day.
Polar explorers have been poisoned by the vitamin A in a polar bear's liver.
explanations.art: A salt packet marked 'iodised', a child playing in midday sun, and a health worker handing a strip of red tablets to a pregnant woman.

explanations.concept: Fibre, water and too much of a good thing
explanations.definition: Fibre and water are not burned for energy, yet the body cannot stay well without them. Sugar, salt and fat are needed, yet too much of them causes illness.
explanations.description: Fibre is the part of plants that human enzymes cannot digest. It holds water, so faeces stay soft and pass easily. The bacteria in the large intestine feed on fibre. Whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit hold fibre. Maida, white sugar and oil hold almost none. Water is lost all day in urine, sweat and breath, so it must be replaced all day. Pale yellow urine is a sign of enough water. A diet can also be unbalanced by too much. Extra sugar and fat are stored as body fat. Sweet drinks, fried snacks and packet foods give a lot of energy and salt, with few vitamins or minerals. A person can therefore be overweight and anaemic at once. India now has both problems, sometimes in the same family.
examples: Whole wheat atta leaves brown flakes of bran in a fine sieve. Maida leaves none.
A 250 millilitre bottle of a sweet fizzy drink holds about 6 teaspoons of sugar.
A child who drinks too little water on a hot day gets a headache and dark yellow urine.
explanations.art: A sieve of bran flakes, a tumbler of water and a small heap of six sugar cubes beside a fizzy drink bottle.

explanations.definition: Doctors agree that kwashiorkor comes from a poor diet in early childhood. They do not agree on exactly what in that diet causes the swelling.
explanations.description: Two children can eat the same poor diet. One gets the swelling of kwashiorkor, and the other becomes thin with marasmus. Too little protein does not fully explain this. Scientists are still testing other causes.
examples: Cicely Williams described kwashiorkor in the Gold Coast, now Ghana, in 1933.
In Malawi, scientists studied twins of whom only one had kwashiorkor.

perspectives.who: Dr Cicely Williams, a doctor in the Gold Coast, in 1933 and 1935
perspectives.explanation: She saw the illness in children who had been weaned on to maize porridge when a new baby came. She said some needed part of the diet was missing, most likely protein. Milk cured many of the children.

perspectives.who: Dr C. Gopalan in Hyderabad in 1968, and Dr Michael Golden in the 1980s
perspectives.explanation: Gopalan compared the diets of children who got kwashiorkor and children who got marasmus. He found no clear difference. Golden proposed that harmful molecules damage the body when protective nutrients are missing.

perspectives.who: Michelle Smith, Jeffrey Gordon and their team, in 2013
perspectives.explanation: They studied 317 pairs of twins in Malawi. In some pairs only one twin got kwashiorkor on the same food. The ill twin's gut microbes were different. Mice given those microbes and the same poor diet lost weight. So gut microbes may be one of the causes.

explanations.art: Two small twin children side by side, one with swollen feet and one without, eating from the same bowl.

agreed.text: A person can eat enough food and still fall ill from the lack of one nutrient.
agreed.evidence: In 1747 James Lind treated twelve sailors with scurvy on one ship. All ate the same meals. Only the two who were also given oranges and lemons recovered quickly.

agreed.text: Too little iodine causes goitre, and iodised salt prevents it.
agreed.evidence: From 1956, Dr V. Ramalingaswami's team compared villages in the Kangra valley. After about five or six years, goitre had fallen by about half or more where the salt was iodised, and not where it was plain.

agreed.text: The eye needs vitamin A to see in dim light.
agreed.evidence: In 1933 George Wald found vitamin A in the retina. Later work showed that the light-catching substance of the rods is built from it.

agreed.text: Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron from plant foods. Tea with a meal lowers the amount absorbed.
agreed.evidence: In the 1970s, scientists gave volunteers meals with iron atoms that could be traced. Less iron was absorbed with tea, and more with vitamin C.

agreed.text: A cereal and a pulse eaten together give better protein than either alone.
agreed.evidence: Chemists measured the amino acids in grains and pulses. Cereals are low in lysine and pulses are low in methionine, and each has plenty of the other.

agreed.text: Growing children need more food for each kilogram of body weight than adults do.
agreed.evidence: Nutrition scientists have measured the energy that people of each age use in a day. India's National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad publishes the figures.

challenging.claim: If you eat until you are full, you get everything your body needs.
challenging.for: Hunger is the body's signal for food, and it stops when the stomach is full.
challenging.against: Fullness reports energy and bulk. No feeling reports vitamins or minerals. Sailors with scurvy and rice eaters with beriberi had full stomachs.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about food, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Kwashiorkor is caused by too little protein, and nothing else.
challenging.for: It appears in children weaned on to starchy porridge, and milk often cures it.
challenging.against: Children on the same diet do not all get it. Gut microbes, infections and missing protective nutrients may each play a part.
challenging.context: This is an idea found in many school textbooks. Scientists now argue about it.

challenging.claim: Vitamin tablets are as good as food, and more vitamins are always better.
challenging.for: Tablets do cure deficiency diseases, and health workers give them for that.
challenging.against: Too much vitamin A or iron is a poison. Large studies find little benefit from extra vitamin tablets for people who eat a varied diet. Whole foods also carry fibre and many other substances.
challenging.context: This is a claim made in many advertisements, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Big doses of vitamin C stop you catching colds.
challenging.who: Linus Pauling, a chemist who won two Nobel Prizes, in a book in 1970.
challenging.for: Vitamin C is needed by the cells that fight infection, and Pauling was a great chemist.
challenging.against: Many careful trials have tested it since. For most people, daily vitamin C does not prevent colds. It may shorten a cold slightly.
challenging.context: This is a claim by a famous scientist that later tests did not support.

challenging.claim: Spinach is the best food for iron.
challenging.who: A common belief, helped by cartoons.
challenging.for: Spinach, called palak in Hindi, does hold iron.
challenging.against: Spinach also holds substances that grip the iron, so the gut absorbs little of it. Bajra, kala chana, rajma, eggs and meat give iron that is absorbed better.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about one food, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: India's Green Revolution ended hunger in India.
challenging.for: From the 1960s, new wheat and rice gave far bigger harvests, and India stopped depending on grain from abroad.
challenging.against: Fields of pulses and millets gave way to wheat and rice. Energy became cheap, but iron, protein and vitamins did not. M. S. Swaminathan, who helped lead the work, later called for farming that also ends hidden hunger.
challenging.context: This is a common account of how India came to grow enough grain. Scientists and farmers argue about what it left out.

big_questions.q: The vitamin A in your eye began as carotene in a plant. Is the substance that catches dim light yours, or the plant's?
big_questions.hint: Your gut wall split the carotene and your eye built the substance. The plant made the starting material.

big_questions.q: Your body cannot make vitamin C, but a goat's body can. Why might a body lose the power to make something it needs?
big_questions.hint: Our ancestors ate fruit and leaves every day. What happens to a tool that is never needed?

big_questions.q: You feel hunger and thirst. Why is there no feeling for 'short of iodine'?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long each shortage takes to harm you, and how our ancestors could have answered it.

big_questions.q: India grows enough grain for everyone, yet more than half of its women are anaemic. Is that a problem of growing, of sharing or of knowing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is grown, what it costs, who eats last in a family, and what people know.

big_questions.q: Is giving everyone the same amount of food fair?
big_questions.hint: Compare what a child of two, a girl of fourteen and a grandmother each need.

big_questions.q: Cooks paired rice with dal long before anyone had heard of amino acids. How can people know that something works before they know why?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many meals and how many generations a kitchen has had to try things.

story.title: The Equal Ladle
story.note: Ammu, Saramma, Jancy, Minnu, Rosamma, Sneha and the others are made up. These facts are real: in August 2018 floods covered much of Kerala, and Chengannur on the Pamba river was among the worst-hit towns. More than ten lakh people lived for days in relief camps, many of them in schools. Kanji, which is rice boiled soft in plenty of water, and payar, which is green gram, were common camp meals. A breastfeeding mother needs about 600 kilocalories more each day. A two-year-old has a small stomach and needs small meals often.
text: In August 2018 the Pamba river came into Ammu's house, and her family went to live in a school.

The school stood on high ground in Chengannur. Four hundred people slept in its classrooms. In the yard, under a blue plastic sheet, Saramma chechi cooked for all of them in two pots as wide as cartwheels. One pot held kanji, which is rice boiled soft in plenty of water. The other held payar, green gram cooked with salt and coconut.
Ammu was eleven, and she wanted a job. Saramma gave her the payar ladle.
On the first evening a man in the line pointed at the plate ahead of his. "She got more than I did," he said. Ammu looked. Perhaps the woman had. Ammu's ears went hot.
That night she made a rule. Every person in the line would get one ladle, filled level. She told Saramma. "Then nobody can say it is unfair."
Saramma was scraping the kanji pot. "Try it," she said.
The next day Ammu served four hundred level ladles. She scraped the top of each one flat with a spoon. Nobody in the line complained.
But afterwards she saw four things.

Jancy came back to the pot with an empty plate and her baby, Appu, on her shoulder. "Is there any left?" she asked. "One ladle each, chechi," said Ammu. "That is the rule." Jancy nodded and went away.
Minnu, who was two, got a level ladle like everyone else. She ate five spoonfuls and pushed the plate away. Two hours later she was crying for food, and the pots were empty.
Kuttan appachan, who was eighty, ate slowly from the edge of his plate. He left half his payar. "My teeth," he said, and he smiled as if it were his fault.

At dusk the cleaning party came back. All day they had shovelled river mud out of houses. Rosamma had carried the mud away in buckets, two at a time. She ate her share in a minute. Then she sat on the steps with her head on her knees.

Ammu washed the plates that night. The slop bucket beside her was heavy with payar that people had left. She had to drag it to the pit with both hands. At the top of the steps, Rosamma was still sitting with her head down.
Ammu stood between the bucket and the steps. Food had been thrown away, and people were still hungry. Both things had come out of the same pot, by the same ladle.

She fetched her school notebook and drew a line down a page. On the left she wrote the names of those who had left food. Minnu. Appachan. Two of the old women from Room 3. On the right she wrote the names of those who were still hungry. Jancy. Rosamma. The others who had shovelled. Her cousin Sneha, who was fourteen and had grown out of two skirts that year.

She looked at the lists for a long time. The left side was easy. They were small, or they were old. The right side took longer. Rosamma worked with her whole body all day. Sneha was growing. But Jancy was not growing, and she did no shovelling.

Then Appu cried somewhere in the dark. The crying stopped, and Ammu knew he was feeding. Everything Appu was made of came to him through Jancy. Jancy was eating for two bodies, and one of them was growing faster than anyone else in the camp.
In the morning Ammu took the notebook to Saramma. "The ladles were equal," she said. "The people were not."
Saramma read both lists. "So what will you do? It is the same pot."

Ammu had thought about it half the night. "Minnu gets half a ladle at noon and half at four o'clock. Her stomach is as small as her fist. Appachan gets half, mashed, with more kanji water. The ones who shovel get two. Sneha gets one and a half."
"And Jancy?"
"Two. One of them is Appu's."
Saramma counted on her fingers. What the small and the old would leave came to nearly what the others needed. "The pot will do," she said.
That evening the same man stood in the line. He watched Ammu give Jancy a second ladle. "She got two," he said.
"She is feeding two," said Ammu. "Appu takes his share through her."
The man looked at the baby. He looked at Rosamma behind him, with mud up to her elbows. Then he held his own plate back a little. "Half is enough for me," he said. "I sat in the classroom all day."

That night the slop bucket was so light that Ammu carried it with one hand. Minnu had eaten at four, and she was asleep. Rosamma sat on the steps again. This time she was telling a story, and the people around her were laughing.
Ammu rinsed the ladle and hung it on its nail. It was the same ladle, and tomorrow there would be the same two pots. But she would not fill it level for everyone again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Ammu thought that a fair share was the same amount for everyone. Her two lists showed her that bodies need different amounts. A body needs more when it is growing, when it does heavy work, and when it is feeding a baby. A small child needs little at a time, but often. An old person needs less, and softer food. A balanced diet is measured against one person's body.
ask: Ammu gave everyone the same ladle. Why were some people still hungry while others left food?
Jancy was not growing and did no heavy work. Why did her body need more food?
Minnu was hungry again two hours after the meal. What does that tell you about feeding a small child?
Who in your home needs the most food for their size? What makes you think so?

games.title: Missing Nutrient: collect the sets
games.context: This is a card game about deficiency diseases. Each nutrient has three cards: its job, what happens without it, and cheap foods that hold it. You collect all three.

printables.title: 24 cards: three for each of eight nutrients. Print on one side only
items: VITAMIN A. My job: I build the substance in your eyes that catches dim light. I also keep your skin and the lining of your gut strong.
Without me, you cannot see at dusk. This is night blindness. Later the surface of the eye dries.
Find me cheaply in drumstick leaves, carrot, pumpkin, papaya and mango. They hold carotene, and your body turns it into me.
VITAMIN B1. My job: I help your cells get energy out of rice, wheat and sugar.
Without me, the legs turn weak and numb, and the heart grows weak. This is beriberi.
Find me cheaply in unpolished rice, whole wheat atta, ragi, dals and groundnuts. Polishing rice white removes most of me.
VITAMIN C. My job: I help build collagen, the strong threads in skin, gums and blood vessels. I also help the gut absorb iron.
Without me, gums bleed, teeth loosen and wounds stay open. This is scurvy.
Find me cheaply in amla, guava, lemon, tomato, raw cabbage and sprouted moong. Long boiling in water washes me out.
VITAMIN D. My job: I help your gut absorb calcium from food.
Without me, a child's bones stay soft and the legs bend. This is rickets.
Your skin makes me when the Sun is high in the sky. Egg yolk, fish and fortified milk and oil hold some of me.
IRON. My job: I sit inside haemoglobin, the red substance in blood that carries oxygen.
Without me, a person is tired, breathless and pale. This is anaemia.
Find me cheaply in bajra, ragi, kala chana, rajma and green leaves. Eggs, fish and meat hold me too. Lemon helps, and tea with the meal hinders.
IODINE. My job: The thyroid gland in your neck uses me to make the hormone that sets how fast your cells work.
Without me, the thyroid swells into a lump at the front of the neck. This is goitre.
Find me in iodised salt, and in fish and other food from the sea.
CALCIUM. My job: I make bones and teeth hard. Nerves and muscles use me too.
Without me, bones and teeth grow weak and break easily.
Find me cheaply in ragi, sesame seeds, milk, curd, drumstick leaves and small fish eaten with their bones.
PROTEIN. My job: I build muscle, skin, blood and hair. A growing body needs a lot of me.
Without enough of me and of food as a whole, a small child stops growing. The feet and face may swell. This is kwashiorkor.
Find me cheaply in dal with rice, roasted chana, groundnuts, soya, egg and milk.

Vitamin C: its job card, 'gums bleed, teeth loosen', and 'amla, guava, lemon'.
Vitamin D: its job card, 'a child's bones stay soft', and 'your skin makes me'.

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down as a pile.
A set is three cards for one nutrient: the job card, the 'Without me' card and the 'Find me' card.
On your turn, ask one player for a nutrient you already hold a card for. Say, for example, 'Do you have a card for iron?'
If that player has one, they give it to you and you ask again. If not, take a card from the pile, and your turn ends.
When you hold all three cards of a set, lay them down and read them aloud. The others check them on the answer sheet.
If the set is wrong, take the cards back and miss your next turn.
The game ends when all eight sets are down. The player with the most sets wins.
Playing alone? Spread all 24 cards face up. Sort them into eight sets as fast as you can. Check with the answer sheet, and then try to beat your time.

flow.parent: A child often asks for a card by its disease. That is fine. The link from the nutrient's job to the disease is the point of the game.

flow.kid: Count your sets. Which foods are on more than one card?

check.q: Ragi appears on the cards for vitamin B1, iron and calcium. What does that show?
options: One cheap food can supply several nutrients
Ragi is the only food a person needs
check.why: Ragi, drumstick leaves and dals each hold several nutrients, so a few cheap foods can fill many gaps. If you chose 'the only food', remember that ragi has almost no vitamin C or vitamin A.

flow.context: This is the last step of Missing Nutrient. You count your sets and look for foods that supply several nutrients.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Each player takes a person card and reads the needs aloud. Deal 4 food cards to each player.
flow.say: Read your person card. Which need is the biggest number? Why might this person need so much of that?
flow.kid: Take a person card. Read the needs. Which number is biggest? Why?

ask.q: Why does your person need so much of that nutrient?
good: The girl of 14 will soon lose some blood each month, so she needs iron.
The woman on the building site uses her muscles all day, so she needs energy.
The grandmother's bones lose calcium with age.

flow.context: This is the first step of Fill the Plate. You take a person card and read what that person needs.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Each player keeps a running total on a plate sheet. Stop when someone says 'Balanced' and the plate checks out.

flow.kid: Take a card. Put one on your plate or throw one away. Add up your points.

flow.do: Lay the winning plate beside another player's plate. Compare them. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Put two plates side by side. Would the first plate do for the second person? What would be missing, or too much?
flow.kid: Compare two plates. Would your plate suit the other person? Why?

check.q: A plate holds 7 cards. Why does a packet of chips make the plate harder to balance?
