experiments.title: The Dark Room Test: how long do your eyes take to see in dim light?
experiments.context: In this experiment you go from bright light into a dark room. You time how long each of three things takes to appear. It shows how the eye rebuilds the substance that catches dim light, which is built from vitamin A.
experiments.question: After bright light, you sit in a nearly dark room. How many seconds do your eyes take to see a white towel, a steel tumbler and a dark book? Does a short flash of light undo the change in both eyes, or only in the eye that saw it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see all three things at once, or one after another? How long will the dark book take? If one eye stays covered during a flash of light, will the two eyes see the same afterwards? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Sit in the same bright place for 2 minutes before each try. Use the same room, the same three things and the same places for them. Keep the door closed in the same way each time, so the room is equally dark. The person with the clock stands outside the door, so that no phone screen lights the room. Only one thing changes: who is being tested.
results_table: Seconds until the child sees it
Seconds until the grown-up sees it

materials.item: a room that can be made nearly dark, such as a bathroom with no window, or any room at night with the curtains drawn
a white towel or white hanky
a steel tumbler
a book with a dark cover
a low stool or a mat to sit on
a clock or phone that shows seconds, kept outside the room
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: Clear the floor of the dark room, and sit down as soon as you are inside. Do not walk about in the dark. Never look straight at the Sun or at a bright bulb. A grown-up stays just outside the door the whole time.

schedule.what: Sit in bright light, then time how long three things take to appear in a dark room. Repeat with a grown-up, and try the one-eye flash.

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: white towel, steel tumbler and dark book. Write the seconds for the child and for the grown-up. Under the table, write what each eye saw after the flash.

setup.art: A white towel, a steel tumbler and a dark-covered book placed apart on the floor of a small room, with a low stool facing them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up puts a white towel, a steel tumbler and a dark book in the room. The child does not see where.

setup.art: A child sitting beside a bright sunny window, looking at the room and not at the Sun.
setup.caption: 2. Sit in a bright place for 2 minutes.

setup.art: A child sitting on a stool in a nearly dark room with a thin line of light under the closed door, and a grown-up outside the door holding a clock.
setup.caption: 3. Sit in the dark room. Call out when you see each thing. The grown-up outside writes the seconds.

setup.art: A child in a dim room holding one palm firmly over one closed eye while a ceiling light is on.
setup.caption: 4. Cover one eye. The light goes on for 10 seconds and off again. Compare your two eyes.

flow.do: Make the room nearly dark, with only a thin line of light under the door. Put the towel, the tumbler and the book on the floor, about a metre from the stool. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will go from bright light into a dark room where I have put three things. Will you see them all at once? How long will the darkest one take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three things wait in a dark room. Will you see them at once? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might a dark book take longer to see than a white towel?
good: White things send back more light.
My eyes need time to get used to the dark.
The book is nearly the same shade as the dark room.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Check the room first with your own eyes: after five minutes inside you should just be able to make out the dark book. If you cannot, open the door by a finger's width.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dark Room Test. You guess how long your eyes will take to see three things in a dark room.

flow.do: Your child sits for 2 minutes near a sunny window or under a bright light, looking around the room. They must not look at the Sun or the bulb.
flow.say: Sit here in the bright light for two minutes. Look around the room, and never straight at the Sun or the bulb.
flow.kid: Sit in bright light for two minutes. Do not look at the Sun.
flow.parent: Bright light breaks down the dim-light substance in the eyes. Do not explain this yet. Two minutes is enough.
flow.context: In this step of the Dark Room Test you sit in bright light for two minutes.

flow.do: Lead your child into the dark room and seat them on the stool. Close the door and start the clock. Stand outside. Each time they call out a thing they can see, write the seconds. Stop after 10 minutes.
flow.say: Sit still and keep your eyes open. Call out the moment you can see something, and tell me what it is. I am right outside the door.
flow.kid: Sit still in the dark. Call out when you see each thing. Say what it is.

check.q: In the Dark Room Test, why does the person with the phone stand outside the door?
options: So no phone light reaches the child's eyes
check.why: A lit screen would light the room and break down the dim-light substance again, so the times would be wrong. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test keeps everything the same except the one thing being tested.

flow.parent: Most children see the white towel within a minute and the tumbler in one to four minutes. The dark book takes several minutes. If everything shows in the first 20 seconds, the room is too bright. Block the gap under the door with a cloth and start again from the bright light.
flow.context: In this step of the Dark Room Test you sit in the dark room. You call out when you see each thing.

flow.do: Stay in the dark room together. Your child closes one eye and presses a palm over it. Switch the light on for 10 seconds, then off. Your child now looks at the book with each eye in turn.
flow.say: Close your left eye and cover it with your palm. I will switch the light on for ten seconds. Now it is off. Look at the book with your right eye only. Now with your left eye only.
flow.kid: Cover one eye with your palm. The light goes on, then off. Look with each eye.
flow.parent: The covered eye still sees the book. The eye that saw the light sees almost nothing for some minutes. Let your child describe it before you say anything.
flow.context: In this step of the Dark Room Test one eye stays covered during a short flash of light. Then you compare the two eyes.

flow.do: Now your child times you. Sit in the bright light for 2 minutes, then in the dark room. Your child stands outside with the clock and writes your seconds.
flow.say: Now you time me in the same way. Do you think my eyes will be faster or slower than yours? Why?
flow.kid: Now time your grown-up. Will their eyes be faster or slower? Why?
flow.parent: To save time, stop when you see the dark book. Eyes usually get slower at this with age, so a grown-up often takes longer than a child.
flow.context: In this step of the Dark Room Test a grown-up takes the same test, and the child keeps the time.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Why did only the uncovered eye lose its sight in the dark?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The covered eye could still see the book, and the other eye could not. What does that tell you?
good: The light changed something inside the eye that saw it.
The change happens in each eye by itself.
The dark did not change. My eye changed.

ask.q: A person short of vitamin A waits in the dark, and the book never appears. Why?
good: Their eyes cannot rebuild enough of the substance that catches dim light.
The substance is made from vitamin A.

flow.parent: The reason: the cells that see in dim light are packed with a substance called rhodopsin. Bright light breaks it down. In the dark the eye rebuilds it over 20 to 30 minutes, so dim things appear one by one. The flash broke it down again, but only in the eye that saw the flash. The eye builds rhodopsin from vitamin A. A person short of vitamin A cannot rebuild enough, and stays nearly blind in dim light. That is night blindness. A slow time in this test does not mean your child lacks vitamin A. The time depends mostly on how dark the room is.
flow.think: Drivers at night are told not to look at the headlights of cars coming towards them. Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Dark Room Test. You say what your times and the one-eye flash show about how eyes see in dim light.

experiments.title: The Cooking Water Test: where does the vitamin C go when cabbage is boiled?
experiments.context: In this experiment you boil chopped cabbage and test the water for vitamin C. The test uses a blue liquid made from iodine and starch. Vitamin C makes the blue colour disappear. It shows what happens to a vitamin when a vegetable is boiled and the water is thrown away.
experiments.question: When cabbage is boiled for 10 minutes, does vitamin C move out of the cabbage into the water? Does the same thing happen when raw cabbage only sits in cold water for 10 minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Three liquids will be tested: plain water, water that raw cabbage sat in, and water that cabbage was boiled in. Which will clear the blue liquid in the fewest teaspoons? Will any of them not clear it at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 1 cup of chopped cabbage and 1 cup of water for the cold soak. Use the same amounts for the boiling. Leave both for 10 minutes. After boiling, add plain water to bring the cooking water back up to 1 cup, because some has boiled away. Cool it to room temperature, because the blue colour fades in hot liquid. Put the same amount of blue liquid, 2 tablespoons, in every bowl. Add each test liquid one level teaspoon at a time, and stir the same way. Only one thing changes: which liquid you add.
results_table: Teaspoons until the blue was gone (stop at 10)

materials.item: fresh cabbage, chopped fine, 2 cups (capsicum or cauliflower also work)
drinking water, about 4 cups
a small steel vessel for boiling, and a steel bowl for the cold soak
rice water, 2 tablespoons: the cloudy water poured off when rice is cooked, cooled. Or a pinch of cornflour boiled in half a cup of water, cooled
povidone-iodine, the brown antiseptic liquid sold at any chemist, or tincture of iodine
small white bowls or steel bowls, standing on a sheet of white paper
a teaspoon, a tablespoon, a tea strainer and a tumbler for mixing
half a lemon

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the boiling and handles the iodine. Iodine stains skin and cloth, and it must never be swallowed. Nobody tastes anything from the test bowls. Pour the test bowls down the sink afterwards and wash them.

schedule.what: Boil one cup of cabbage and soak another in cold water. Then test both waters, and plain water, with the blue liquid.

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: lemon juice, plain water, cold cabbage water and boiled cabbage water. Write how many teaspoons each took to clear the blue, and the colour at the end.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Teaspoons until the blue was gone

setup.art: Two equal heaps of finely chopped cabbage on a steel plate, one being tipped into a vessel on a stove and the other into a bowl of cold water.
setup.caption: 1. Put 1 cup of chopped cabbage in 1 cup of cold water. A grown-up boils another cup of cabbage in 1 cup of water. Leave both for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring cabbage cooking water through a tea strainer into a tumbler, with a second tumbler of cold-soak water beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Strain both waters. Top the boiled water up to 1 cup and let it cool.

setup.art: A tumbler of pale blue liquid beside a small brown bottle and a spoon of cloudy rice water.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up mixes water, rice water and 3 drops of iodine to make a pale blue liquid.

setup.art: Four white bowls of pale blue liquid on white paper, with a child adding a teaspoon of clear liquid to one and the blue fading.
setup.caption: 4. Add each test liquid one teaspoon at a time. Count the teaspoons until the blue is gone.

flow.do: Chop the cabbage fine and measure out two level cups. Tell your child the three liquids that will be tested. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Vitamin C makes a certain blue liquid lose its colour. We will test plain water, cold cabbage water and boiled cabbage water. Which will clear the blue fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three liquids will be tested. Which will clear the blue fastest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where do you think the vitamin C in cabbage is before cooking?
good: Inside the cabbage.
In the juice of the leaves.
Inside the cells of the leaf.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect boiling to destroy the vitamin and leave none anywhere.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cooking Water Test. You guess which of three liquids holds the most vitamin C, before you test.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 cup of cabbage in a bowl with 1 cup of cold water, and stir it twice. 2. Boil the other cup of cabbage in 1 cup of water for 10 minutes, without a lid. 3. Note the time for both.
flow.say: Both heaps of cabbage get one cup of water and ten minutes. One sits cold, and I boil the other. Why must the amounts and the time be the same?
flow.kid: Put one cup of cabbage in cold water. A grown-up boils the other. Wait ten minutes.
flow.parent: Equal cabbage, equal water and equal time make the test fair. Then only the heat differs between the two.
flow.context: In this step of the Cooking Water Test one cup of cabbage sits in cold water and another is boiled.

flow.do: 1. Strain each water into its own tumbler and keep the cabbage for dinner. 2. Add plain water to the boiled water to bring it back to 1 cup. 3. Stand that tumbler in a bowl of cold water until it is cool to touch.
flow.say: Some water boiled away, so I will top this tumbler up to one cup again. We must also cool it, because the blue colour fades in hot liquid.
flow.kid: Strain both waters. Top up the boiled one to one cup. Cool it.

check.q: In the Cooking Water Test, why is the boiled water topped up to 1 cup again?
options: So both waters are the same amount
check.why: Some water boiled away. Less water would make the liquid stronger and the test unfair. Topping it up makes the two waters equal in amount, so only the heating differs. If you chose taste or speed, remember that this water is being tested and not eaten.

flow.context: In this step of the Cooking Water Test you strain the two cabbage waters and cool the boiled one.

flow.do: 1. In a tumbler, mix 1 cup of water with 1 tablespoon of rice water. 2. Add 3 drops of iodine and stir. The liquid should be pale blue, and you should see through it. 3. Put 2 tablespoons in each of 4 bowls on white paper.
flow.say: Iodine turns the starch in rice water blue. Vitamin C undoes that. I will put the same amount of blue liquid in each bowl.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes rice water and iodine. It turns blue. Pour the same amount into four bowls.
flow.parent: If the liquid is dark like ink, add water until it is pale. If it stays brown, add a little more rice water. A pale blue makes the test sensitive enough for cabbage.
flow.context: In this step of the Cooking Water Test a grown-up makes the pale blue test liquid.

flow.do: 1. First squeeze lemon juice into bowl one, drop by drop, to see the blue vanish. 2. Add plain water to bowl two, one level teaspoon at a time, stirring each time. Stop at 10. 3. Do the same with the cold cabbage water and the boiled cabbage water. Write each count.
flow.say: Lemon juice is full of vitamin C, so watch what it does first. Now add each test liquid one teaspoon at a time. Count the teaspoons until the blue is gone.
flow.kid: Add lemon drops and watch. Then add each liquid by teaspoons. Count until the blue goes.
flow.parent: Plain water makes the blue paler but does not clear it. That bowl shows what 'still blue' looks like. Compare the other bowls with it on the white paper.
flow.context: In this step of the Cooking Water Test you add each liquid to the blue liquid by teaspoons, and count.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Where is the vitamin C now?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The boiled cabbage water cleared the blue in the fewest teaspoons. What does that tell you?
good: It holds the most vitamin C of the three.
The vitamin C moved from the cabbage into the water.
If we throw this water away, we throw the vitamin away.

ask.q: How could a cook keep that vitamin C in the meal?
good: Use the cooking water in sambar, rasam or dal.
Cook with very little water and a lid.
Eat some cabbage raw.

flow.parent: In most kitchens the boiled water clears the blue in 1 to 3 teaspoons. The cold water takes many more, or does not clear it. Plain water never does. Write what you really found. The reason: vitamin C dissolves in water. Heat softens the walls of the leaf's cells, so the vitamin leaks out into the water. Some vitamin C is also destroyed by long heating. A few other substances from cabbage clear a little iodine too, so the count is a rough measure. The cabbage and the rest of the cooking water can go into tonight's dinner.
flow.think: Rasam, sambar and kanji all keep the water that the food was cooked in. What does that save?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cooking Water Test. You say what your teaspoon counts show about where the vitamin C went.

experiments.title: The Short Shadow Test: when is the Sun high enough for skin to make vitamin D?
experiments.context: In this experiment you measure the shadow of an upright pencil at four times in one day. Skin makes vitamin D well only when the Sun is high. A short shadow is the sign of a high Sun.
experiments.question: At which times of day is the shadow of an upright pencil shorter than the pencil? For how many hours of the day does that last?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. You will measure at 8 in the morning, 10, 12 noon and 4 in the afternoon. At each time, will the shadow be longer or shorter than the pencil? At which of these times will it be shortest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same pencil each time and stand it straight up, not leaning. Use the same flat place each time. Measure the shadow from the foot of the pencil to the tip of the shadow. Only one thing changes: the time of day.
results_table: Length of the shadow in centimetres
Shorter or longer than the pencil?

materials.item: a new, unsharpened pencil
a lump of atta dough or clay the size of a lemon, to hold the pencil upright
a ruler or a measuring tape
a flat place that gets direct sunlight for most of the day: a balcony floor, a terrace or a wide window sill
a notebook page and a pencil for writing

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun. Each measurement takes two minutes, so there is no need to stay out long. On a terrace, a grown-up comes along.

schedule.what: Measure the pencil's shadow at about 8 in the morning, 10, 12 noon and 4 in the afternoon. Then compare each shadow with the pencil's height.

experiments.record: Write the height of the pencil at the top of the page. Draw a table with four rows, one for each time. Write the length of the shadow, and 'shorter' or 'longer'.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for a pencil 18 centimetres tall
cols: Shorter or longer than the pencil?

setup.art: An unsharpened pencil standing straight up in a lump of dough on a sunny balcony floor, with a ruler beside it showing its height.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a pencil straight up in a lump of dough. Measure how tall it stands.

setup.art: The same pencil casting a long shadow across the floor, and a child measuring the shadow from the foot of the pencil to its tip.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the shadow from the foot of the pencil to the tip of the shadow.

setup.art: The same pencil at noon with a very short shadow, and a notebook table with four rows beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Measure again at 10, at 12 noon and at 4. Write 'shorter' or 'longer' each time.

flow.do: At about 8 in the morning, stand the pencil upright in the dough on the flat, sunny place. Measure how tall it stands above the floor. Ask for the guess and the reason. Then measure the first shadow.
flow.say: We will measure this pencil's shadow four times today. At which times will the shadow be shorter than the pencil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand the pencil up. When will the shadow be shorter than the pencil? Why?

ask.q: What makes a shadow long or short?
good: How high the Sun is in the sky.
A low Sun makes a long shadow.
The time of day.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If the place is in shade at 8, measure as soon as the Sun reaches it. Write that time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Short Shadow Test. You stand a pencil upright, guess, and measure the first shadow.

flow.do: Measure the shadow again at about 10, at 12 noon and at 4 in the afternoon. Each time, check that the pencil is upright. Write the length, and 'shorter' or 'longer'.
flow.say: Measure from the foot of the pencil to the tip of the shadow. Is the shadow shorter or longer than the pencil now?
flow.kid: Measure the shadow at 10, 12 and 4. Write shorter or longer each time.
flow.wait: Come back at about 10, 12 noon and 4 in the afternoon
flow.parent: If the Sun leaves your spot in the afternoon, use a second spot for the last measurement and note it. On a cloudy day with no clear shadow, wait for a sunny day.
flow.context: In this step of the Short Shadow Test you measure the pencil's shadow three more times during the day.

flow.do: Look at the four rows together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Look at your four shadows. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why it happened.

check.q: A pencil's shadow is longer than the pencil. Where is the Sun?
check.why: A low Sun throws long shadows, as at sunrise and sunset. A high Sun throws short ones. If you chose 'behind a cloud', remember that a clear shadow needs direct sunlight.

flow.context: In this step of the Short Shadow Test you compare the four shadows with the height of the pencil.

flow.do: After your child has answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Skin makes vitamin D only in strong sunlight. Some doctors use the short shadow as a rough sign of that. At which hours could your skin make vitamin D today?
flow.kid: Skin makes vitamin D when shadows are short. When was that today?

ask.q: A baby is kept indoors behind closed glass windows all winter. Why might the baby get rickets?
good: Glass blocks the rays that make vitamin D.
The baby's skin gets no direct strong sunlight.
Without vitamin D the gut absorbs too little calcium.

flow.parent: The rays that make vitamin D are a kind of ultraviolet light. When the Sun is low, the air absorbs most of them. A shadow shorter than the thing that casts it means the Sun is high enough. This is a rule of thumb, not an exact line. In north India in December, the shadow may stay longer than the pencil all day. That is a real result. People there make little vitamin D in winter. Window glass blocks these rays too. Ten to fifteen minutes of sun on bare arms and legs, a few times a week, is the usual advice. Darker skin needs longer. Scientists still argue about the exact minutes.
flow.think: India is a sunny country, yet many people here are short of vitamin D. What might keep the sunlight off their skin?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Short Shadow Test. You work out at which hours the Sun was high enough for skin to make vitamin D.

activities.title: One Day's Needs: from two spoons of protein to a tiny amount of iodine
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You lay out the weight of four nutrients that a child of ten needs in one day. You use sugar, a moong seed and a speck of chalk dust only to show how much each nutrient weighs. The sugar, the seed and the chalk dust are not the nutrients themselves.

materials.item: a dark plate or a sheet of dark paper
sugar, 2 heaped tablespoons
whole green moong seeds
table salt, a pinch
a knife, for the grown-up, and 4 small paper labels

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the moong seed.
activities.record: Draw the four heaps and write the unit under each: grams, milligrams or micrograms.

setup.art: A dark plate with a heap of two heaped tablespoons of sugar on the left and one green moong seed next to the heap.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 heaped tablespoons of sugar on a dark plate. Put one moong seed beside the sugar.

setup.art: The same plate with half a moong seed and a speck of chalk dust added in a row, each with a small paper label.
setup.caption: 2. Add half a moong seed and a speck of chalk dust. Label all four with the nutrient they stand for.

flow.do: Ask the question below before you put anything on the plate. Write down the answer and the reason.
flow.say: Your body needs protein, vitamin C, iron and iodine every day. Which do you think it needs the most of? Which the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which nutrient do you need most of each day? Which least? Why?
flow.parent: Any answer with a reason is a good start. Do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Day's Needs. You guess which nutrients the body needs in large and in tiny amounts.

flow.do: 1. Heap 2 heaped tablespoons of sugar on the plate. 2. Put one moong seed beside the sugar. 3. Cut a second moong seed in half and put down one half. 4. Your child taps a piece of chalk to make a speck of chalk dust and puts it on the plate. 5. Label the four: protein, vitamin C, iron, iodine.
flow.say: This heap of sugar weighs about 30 grams. That is the same as the weight of protein you need in a day. One moong seed weighs about the same as the vitamin C you need in a day. Half a seed weighs about the same as the iron you need. A speck of chalk dust weighs about the same as the iodine you need. None of these things contain those nutrients here. They only show how much each one weighs.
flow.kid: Put down the sugar and a moong seed. Add half a seed and a speck of chalk dust. Label them.
flow.parent: The sugar, the seed and the chalk dust only show weights. The real nutrients look different. The figures are rounded: 30 grams of protein, 50 milligrams of vitamin C, 16 to 28 milligrams of iron, 100 micrograms of iodine.
flow.context: In this step of One Day's Needs you lay out the weights of four nutrients for one day.

flow.do: Look at the four heaps together. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the plate. The a speck of chalk dust stand for your iodine. If you got no iodine for a year, would you notice at dinner? What might happen to your body?
flow.kid: The speck of chalk dust stand for your iodine. Would you notice if you got none?

ask.q: Why can a person be short of iodine or iron without knowing?
good: The amount is too small to see or taste.
You still feel full.
The harm comes slowly.

check.q: A child needs 30 grams of protein and 100 micrograms of iodine a day. Which matters more?
options: Both: a lack of either causes illness
Protein, because the amount is bigger
Iodine, because the amount is smaller
check.why: The amount needed says nothing about how much a nutrient matters. Too little protein stops growth, and too little iodine swells the thyroid. If you chose one of them, remember that each does a job the other cannot do.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Day's Needs. You compare the four heaps and ask what happens when the smallest is missing.

activities.title: Seven People, One Pot: who needs what?
activities.context: In this activity you take tonight's family meal and change it for seven different people. You use a table of how much energy, protein and calcium each person needs in a day.

materials.item: seven paper slips, one for each person in the table
a notebook page and a pencil
the menu of tonight's family meal

activities.record: For each of the seven people, write one thing you would add, one thing you would change, and why.

example_chart.title: What seven people need in one day (rounded figures from India's National Institute of Nutrition)
rows: Woman who works at a desk
Woman who carries loads all day

setup.art: A table of numbers in a notebook with seven rows, and seven small paper slips with a person written on each.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the table. Write each person on a slip.

setup.art: A child drawing a plate for a toddler and a plate for a grandmother side by side, with tonight's pot of sambar and rice in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Pick a slip. Change tonight's meal to suit that person, and say why.

flow.do: Show your child the table. Ask them to find the biggest and the smallest number in the energy column. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the energy column. Who needs the most, and who needs the least? Does the biggest person need the most food?
flow.kid: Look at the energy numbers. Who needs most? Who needs least? Is it by size?

ask.q: The girl of 13 weighs less than the woman at the desk, yet she needs more energy. Why?
good: She is growing.
She is building new bone and muscle.
She moves about more.

flow.parent: The figures are rounded from India's National Institute of Nutrition. They are averages. Real people differ.
flow.context: This is the first step of Seven People, One Pot. You read a table of what seven people need in a day.

flow.do: Work out the energy for each kilogram of body weight for three people: the child of 2, the girl of 10 to 12 and the woman at the desk. Divide the energy by the weight.
flow.say: Divide each person's energy by their weight. That gives the energy for each kilogram of their body. Who needs the most for their size?
flow.kid: Divide energy by weight for three people. Who needs most for their size?

check.q: A child of 2 needs 1,110 kilocalories and weighs 13 kilograms. About how much is that for each kilogram?
check.why: 1,110 divided by 13 is about 85. The woman at the desk needs 1,660 divided by 55, which is about 30. So for each kilogram, the small child needs more than twice as much. If you chose 30, that is the woman's figure.

flow.parent: The answers are about 83 for the child of 2 and about 57 for the girl. The woman's is about 31. Growth is the reason.
flow.context: In this step of Seven People, One Pot you work out three people's energy for each kilogram of weight.

flow.do: Write tonight's meal at the top of a page. Your child picks the slips one at a time. For each person they say what to add or change in tonight's meal, and why.
flow.say: Here is tonight's meal. Pick a slip. What would you add or change for this person? Use the table and what you know about their body.
flow.kid: Pick a slip. Change tonight's meal for that person. Say why.

ask.q: What would you change for the child of 2?
good: Mash it and leave out the chilli.
Give small amounts five or six times a day.
Add ghee or oil, dal and soft vegetables.

ask.q: What would you change for the grandmother?
good: Softer food and a smaller amount.
More curd, ragi or sesame for calcium.
As much dal as before, because she still needs protein.

flow.parent: Good changes: more dal, greens and an extra helping for the pregnant woman. More rice or ragi, water and a little salt for the woman who carries loads. Iron foods with lemon for the girls.
flow.context: In this step of Seven People, One Pot you change tonight's meal for each of seven people.

flow.do: Ask who in your own family is closest to each slip. Ask your child what they would now change on one real plate at home.
flow.say: Who in our family is like one of these seven? Is there one change we could make on a real plate this week?
flow.kid: Who at home is like these people? What one change could we make?
flow.context: This is the last step of Seven People, One Pot. You apply the table to the people in your own family.

activities.title: Find What Was Added: a hunt for fortified foods
activities.context: In this activity you search the kitchen for packets that have a nutrient added on purpose, such as iodised salt. You read how much was added and work out what one day's helping gives you.

materials.item: the kitchen's packets of salt, cooking oil, milk, atta and rice
a notebook page and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: the packet, the nutrient added, and how much the packet says it holds.

setup.art: A packet of salt, a pouch of cooking oil and a packet of milk on a kitchen counter, with a child's finger pointing at small print on the salt packet.
setup.caption: 1. Collect the packets of salt, oil, milk, atta and rice. Look for the words 'iodised' and 'fortified'.

setup.art: A notebook table with three columns and three filled rows, beside a salt packet turned to show its back.
setup.caption: 2. Write the packet, the nutrient added, and the amount printed on the packet.

flow.do: Put the packets on the table. Your child looks on each one for the word 'iodised', the word 'fortified', or a small +F sign. They write what was added.
flow.say: Some foods have a nutrient added on purpose. Look for the words iodised or fortified, or a small plus F sign. What was added to each?
flow.kid: Look for 'iodised', 'fortified' or a +F sign. Write what was added.
flow.parent: Nearly all packet salt in India is iodised. Many oils and milks have vitamins A and D added. Some atta and rice have iron added. If you find only the salt, that is enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find What Was Added. You search the kitchen's packets for added nutrients.

flow.do: On the salt packet, find the line about iodine. It gives parts per million, written ppm. Explain that 30 parts per million means 30 micrograms of iodine in each gram of salt. Work out the iodine in 5 grams of salt, which is about one level teaspoon.
flow.say: This salt says 30 parts per million of iodine. That means 30 micrograms in each gram. A person eats about 5 grams of salt a day. How much iodine is that?
flow.kid: Each gram of salt holds 30 micrograms of iodine. How much is in 5 grams?

check.q: Salt holds 30 micrograms of iodine in each gram. How much iodine is in 5 grams of salt?
check.why: 5 grams hold 5 times 30, which is 150 micrograms. A child needs about 100 micrograms a day, so ordinary salting is enough. If you chose 35, you added where you should have multiplied.

flow.parent: Packets differ. Many say at least 30 parts per million when packed and at least 15 when sold. Some iodine is lost in storage and cooking, so the amount added allows for that.
flow.context: In this step of Find What Was Added you work out one day's iodine from a salt packet.

flow.do: Ask the questions below. Then put the packets back.
flow.say: Why do you think iodine is added to salt, and not to sweets or to ghee? What makes salt a good carrier?
flow.kid: Why is iodine added to salt and not to sweets?

ask.q: What makes salt a good food to carry iodine to everyone?
good: Nearly everyone eats salt every day.
People eat about the same small amount.
It is cheap, so the poorest families buy it too.

flow.parent: Salt is eaten by rich and poor in nearly the same small amount each day. So nobody gets far too much or far too little. More salt is not better for iodine, and too much salt raises blood pressure.
flow.context: This is the last step of Find What Was Added. You ask why salt was chosen to carry iodine.

activities.title: Protein for Ten Rupees: which kitchen food builds the most for the money?
activities.context: In this activity you use your family's own prices for six foods. You work out how many grams of protein ten rupees buys in each. It shows which body-building foods are cheap.

materials.item: the price of six foods, from a shop bill, a shopping app or the packets: a dal, groundnuts, eggs, milk, rice and a packet snack
a notebook page, a pencil and a calculator if you wish

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the food, the price of 100 grams, the protein in 100 grams, and the protein that ten rupees buys.

example_chart.title: Protein in 100 grams of some foods (rounded)

setup.art: A shop bill on a table beside packets of dal, groundnuts and rice, an egg tray and a small packet of chips.
setup.caption: 1. Find the price of six foods. Work out what 100 grams of each costs.

setup.art: A notebook table with four columns, and a child dividing numbers on a calculator.
setup.caption: 2. Divide the protein in 100 grams by the price of 100 grams. Multiply by 10.

flow.do: Name the six foods. Ask your child to put them in order, from the most protein for ten rupees to the least. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Ten rupees can buy some dal, some groundnuts, an egg, some milk, some rice or a small packet of chips. Which gives the most protein for ten rupees? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which food gives the most protein for ten rupees? Guess the order. Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children put egg or milk first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Protein for Ten Rupees. You guess which food gives the most protein for the money.

flow.do: For each food, find the price of 1 kilogram and divide it by 10. That is the price of 100 grams. For a packet snack, use the weight and price on the packet. Write each price in the table.
flow.say: First find what 100 grams of each food costs. A kilogram is ten lots of 100 grams, so divide the price of a kilogram by ten.
flow.kid: Find the price of 1 kilogram. Divide by 10. That is the price of 100 grams.
flow.parent: For eggs, two eggs weigh about 100 grams. For milk, use 100 millilitres. For a 20 gram packet of chips at ten rupees, 100 grams cost fifty rupees.
flow.context: In this step of Protein for Ten Rupees you work out what 100 grams of each food costs.

flow.do: Copy the protein in 100 grams from the table of foods. For each food, divide the protein by the price of 100 grams, then multiply by 10. Write the answer.
flow.say: Divide the grams of protein by the price of 100 grams. That gives the protein for one rupee. Multiply by ten for ten rupees.
flow.kid: Divide protein by price. Multiply by 10. Write the grams for ten rupees.

check.q: Toor dal costs 16 rupees for 100 grams and holds 22 grams of protein. About how much protein does 10 rupees buy?
check.why: 22 divided by 16 is about 1.4 grams for each rupee. Ten rupees buy about 14 grams. If you chose 22, that is the protein in 16 rupees' worth.

flow.context: In this step of Protein for Ten Rupees you work out the protein that ten rupees buys in each food.

flow.do: Put the six foods in order by your results. Compare the order with the guess. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Put the foods in order. Say what you thought the order would be, what you found, and why you think the cheapest protein is cheap.
flow.kid: Put the foods in order. Was your guess right? What surprised you?

ask.q: Rice gives a lot of protein for ten rupees. Why is rice alone still not enough?
good: Rice protein is short of one building unit, lysine.
It needs a pulse beside it.
Rice has little iron or vitamins.

flow.parent: In most Indian kitchens dals, groundnuts, soya and rice come first. Eggs come in the middle. Paneer, milk and packet snacks come last. Prices change, so trust your own numbers.
flow.context: This is the last step of Protein for Ten Rupees. You put the foods in order and compare the order with your guess.

activities.title: Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks: why a cereal and a pulse go together
activities.context: In this activity two kinds of seeds stand for two building units of protein. You build 'bricks' from spoons of rice and spoons of dal, and find out why the two together build more.

materials.item: rajma beans, or any large seeds or buttons of one colour
white chana or groundnuts, or seeds or buttons of a second colour
four paper slips: write RICE on two and DAL on two
a notebook page and a pencil

activities.record: Write how many bricks you built from 2 rice, from 2 dal, and from 1 rice with 1 dal.

setup.art: Two paper slips marked RICE, each with 2 red beans and 6 white chana on it, and two slips marked DAL, each with 6 red beans and 2 white chana.
setup.caption: 1. On each RICE slip put 2 rajma and 6 chana. On each DAL slip put 6 rajma and 2 chana.

setup.art: A child's hands pairing one red bean with one white chana to make a row of pairs on a table.
setup.caption: 2. One brick is one rajma joined with one chana. Build as many bricks as you can.

flow.do: Set out the slips. On each RICE slip put 2 rajma and 6 chana. On each DAL slip put 6 rajma and 2 chana. Explain the rule: one brick of body protein needs one rajma and one chana.
flow.say: The rajma stand for a building unit called lysine. The chana stand for one called methionine. Your body needs one of each to make one brick. Rice is short of lysine, and dal is short of methionine.
flow.kid: A brick needs one rajma and one chana. Rice has few rajma. Dal has few chana.
flow.parent: This is a model. Real proteins use 20 kinds of units, and the body cannot make nine of them. The numbers on the slips are made up to show the pattern.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks. You set up seeds to stand for the building units in rice and in dal.

flow.do: Ask for a guess first. Then your child builds bricks from the two RICE slips together, and counts them. They do the same with the two DAL slips. Last, they use one RICE slip and one DAL slip.
flow.say: Two spoons of rice, two spoons of dal, or one of each: which will build the most bricks? Why do you think so? Now build and count.
flow.kid: Guess which builds most. Build from 2 rice. Then 2 dal. Then 1 of each.

check.q: Two RICE slips hold 4 rajma and 12 chana. A brick needs one of each. How many bricks?
check.why: Each brick needs a rajma, and there are only 4. The other 8 chana have no partner and are left over. If you chose 12 or 16, count how many pairs you can really make.

flow.parent: Two rice slips build 4 bricks. Two dal slips build 4 bricks. One of each builds 8 bricks, with nothing left over.
flow.context: In this step of Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks you build bricks from rice, from dal and from both.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. Then list family dishes that pair a cereal with a pulse.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Which dishes in our kitchen put a cereal and a pulse together?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Name dishes that pair the two.

ask.q: What happened to the leftover seeds when you used rice alone?
good: They had no partner, so they built nothing.
The body burns them for energy but cannot build with them.

ask.q: Which dishes pair a cereal with a pulse?
good: Idli and dosa: rice with urad dal.
Pongal and khichdi: rice with moong dal.
Rajma with rice, dal with roti, puttu with kadala.

flow.parent: The unit in shortest supply sets how much the body can build. Units left without a partner are burned for energy. Milk, egg, fish and soya have both units in good amounts.
flow.context: This is the last step of Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks. You say why rice and dal together build more than either alone.

projects.title: The Good Plate for Less: plan, cost and cook one day's food
projects.context: In this three-day project you plan one full day of balanced meals for yourself. You work out what the food costs, and you cook one of the meals. It shows that a balanced day can cost less than packet food.

materials.item: shop bills, a shopping app or packet prices for your kitchen's foods
a notebook and a pencil
the foods for one meal from your plan
a kitchen with a grown-up to help

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting and all the work at the stove.

schedule.what: List the foods your kitchen has, and plan breakfast, lunch, a snack and dinner against five checks.
Work out the cost of each meal and of the whole day. Compare it with a day of packet snacks.
Cook and eat one meal from the plan with a grown-up, and say what you would change.

projects.record: Write the day's plan as a table: the meal, the foods, the five checks and the cost. On day 3, write one thing you would change.

setup.art: A notebook page with four rows for breakfast, lunch, snack and dinner, and five small tick boxes beside each row.
setup.caption: 1. Plan four meals. Tick five checks: a cereal with a pulse, a green or orange vegetable, a vitamin C food, a calcium food, and water.

setup.art: A child adding up small prices in a notebook beside a shop bill.
setup.caption: 2. Work out what each meal costs. Add up the whole day.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up at a kitchen counter squeezing lemon over a bowl of sprouted moong with chopped tomato.
setup.caption: 3. Cook one meal from your plan with a grown-up.

flow.say: Plan one whole day of food for yourself from what our kitchen has. Then we check it five ways. How much do you think the day will cost? Why?
flow.kid: Plan four meals for yourself. Check them five ways. Guess the cost.
flow.parent: The five checks for the day: a cereal with a pulse at least twice. A dark green or orange vegetable or fruit. A vitamin C food eaten with an iron food. A calcium food such as curd, milk, ragi or sesame. Water through the day.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Good Plate for Less. You plan one day of balanced meals and check the plan five ways.

flow.do: Day 2. For each food in the plan, estimate the amount for one person and work out its cost. Add up each meal and the whole day. Then work out what one packet of chips, one packet of biscuits and one sweet drink would cost together.

flow.kid: Work out the cost of each meal. Add up the day. Compare with packet snacks.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you make the plan

ask.q: Which food in your plan gave the most nourishment for its cost?
good: The dal.
The greens.
The ragi.
The groundnuts or roasted chana.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Good Plate for Less. You work out what your planned day of food costs.

flow.kid: Cook one meal with a grown-up. Say what you found. What would you change?
flow.wait: Do this on the third day
flow.parent: A quick meal to cook: sprouted moong with chopped tomato, onion and lemon. Or ragi dosa with chutney. Praise a plan that was changed after the costing.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Good Plate for Less. You cook one meal from your plan and say what you would change.

challenges.title: Keep the Vitamin: cook cabbage and lose the least
challenges.context: This is a cooking challenge. In the Cooking Water Test, water from boiled cabbage cleared the blue test liquid. That showed vitamin C had moved into the water. Here you design a way to cook cabbage that loses less.
challenges.problem: Cabbage is often boiled in a cup of water, and the water is poured away. Much of the vitamin C goes with it. Design a way to cook 1 cup of chopped cabbage so that as little vitamin C as possible is lost. The cabbage must still be cooked soft enough to eat.
constraints: Use 1 cup of chopped cabbage, as in the Cooking Water Test.
The cabbage must be soft enough to eat within 10 minutes of cooking.
Strain off any water left over and make it up to half a cup with plain water. Cool it and test it with the blue liquid.
The design that needs the most teaspoons to clear the blue has lost the least vitamin C to the water.
materials: 1 cup of chopped cabbage for each design
a steel vessel with a lid
the pale blue test liquid from the Cooking Water Test
general: Cook the cabbage in only 2 tablespoons of water, with the lid on.
Cut the cabbage into big pieces, so less cut surface touches the water.
Cook for a shorter time, until the cabbage is just soft.
creative: Steam the cabbage in a strainer held above boiling water, and test the water below.
Keep all the water in the dish, as in a kootu or a soup, so nothing is poured away.
Stir the cabbage in a spoon of hot oil with no water at all.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way of cooking the cabbage. Test the leftover water, or say why no water is left. Draw your method and write how many teaspoons the water took.

setup.art: A steel vessel with a lid on a stove, with a small amount of chopped cabbage and two tablespoons of water inside.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a way to cook 1 cup of cabbage that should lose less vitamin C.

setup.art: A child adding teaspoons of strained cooking water to a bowl of pale blue liquid and counting.
setup.caption: 2. Test any leftover water with the blue liquid. More teaspoons means less vitamin was lost.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Recall the Cooking Water Test: the boiled water cleared the blue liquid in a few teaspoons. Ask your child for three ideas, and which they expect to work best.
flow.say: In the Cooking Water Test, the vitamin C moved into the water. How could we cook cabbage so that less is lost? Which idea do you think will work best? Why?
flow.kid: The vitamin moved into the water. How could you cook cabbage and lose less?

ask.q: What made the vitamin C leave the cabbage?
good: A lot of water for it to dissolve in.
Heat for a long time.
Many cut surfaces.

flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Vitamin. You think of ways to cook cabbage that lose less vitamin C to the water.

flow.do: Your child chooses one design. A grown-up cooks 1 cup of cabbage that way. Check that it is soft enough to eat.
flow.say: Choose one way and tell me exactly how much water, what size of pieces and how many minutes. I will do the cooking.
flow.kid: Choose your way. Say how much water, what size and how long.
flow.context: In this step of Keep the Vitamin a grown-up cooks one cup of cabbage in the way you designed.

flow.do: Strain off any leftover water. Add plain water to make half a cup, and cool it. Test it with 2 tablespoons of the blue liquid, one teaspoon at a time. Write the count.
flow.say: Now test the water that is left. Add it one teaspoon at a time and count until the blue is gone.
flow.kid: Strain the leftover water. Test it by teaspoons. Count until the blue goes.
flow.parent: If no water is left, nothing was poured away, and that is a good result in itself. A count of 10 with the blue still there means very little vitamin C reached the water.
flow.context: In this step of Keep the Vitamin you test the leftover cooking water with the blue liquid.

flow.do: Compare the count with the count for boiled cabbage water in the Cooking Water Test. Ask the question below. Then eat the cabbage.
flow.say: Compare this count with the boiled water from before. Did your way lose less? What would you change to lose even less?
flow.kid: Compare your count with the boiled water. Did you lose less? What next?

ask.q: Many Indian dishes keep the cooking water in the dish. Name some.
good: Rasam.
Sambar.
Kootu.
Dal.
Kanji.

flow.parent: This test only shows what went into the water. It does not show what heat destroyed. Short cooking with little water, and using the water, saves both.
flow.context: This is the last step of Keep the Vitamin. You compare your result with boiled cabbage water and improve your method.

challenges.title: A Health Mix for a One-Year-Old
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A child of one year needs food that packs a lot of nourishment into a small, soft helping. You design a flour mix that cooks into a porridge for such a child.
challenges.problem: A one-year-old has a stomach about the size of their fist, and few teeth. Yet for each kilogram of body weight they need more than twice the energy of a grown-up. Design a dry mix of roasted, ground foods. Two tablespoons of it, cooked in a cup of water, must make a smooth porridge. The porridge must give energy, protein, iron and calcium.
constraints: Use at least one cereal or millet, at least one pulse, and at least one nut or oilseed.
Everything must be roasted and ground to a fine powder. A baby must never be given whole nuts.
No honey, and no added salt.
The porridge must be smooth, with no lumps, when 2 tablespoons are cooked in 1 cup of water.
The dry mix must keep for two weeks in a closed tin without a fridge.
materials: 4 tablespoons of a cereal or millet: ragi, wheat, rice or bajra
2 tablespoons of a pulse: moong dal, roasted chana or chana dal
1 tablespoon of groundnuts or sesame seeds
a thick pan for roasting and a mixer for grinding
a small tin with a lid
a small pan, water and a spoon for cooking the porridge
general: Ragi, moong dal and groundnuts, each roasted and ground together.
Wheat, roasted chana and sesame seeds.
Rice, moong dal and groundnuts, sieved fine.
creative: Sprout the ragi first, dry the sprouts in the sun, then roast them. Sprouted grain makes a thinner porridge from the same amount of flour.
Add a teaspoon of dried, powdered drumstick leaves for carotene, iron and calcium.
Stir a mashed banana or a spoon of ghee into the cooked porridge for extra energy.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own mix. Write the recipe with amounts. Say which ingredient gives energy, which gives protein, which gives iron and which gives calcium. Cook 2 tablespoons into a porridge and taste it yourself.

setup.art: Three small bowls holding ragi, moong dal and groundnuts beside a thick roasting pan and a mixer jar.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a cereal or millet, a pulse and a nut or oilseed. A grown-up roasts and grinds them.

setup.art: A child stirring a small pan of smooth brown porridge, with a tin of flour mix beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Cook 2 tablespoons of the mix in 1 cup of water. Check that the porridge is smooth.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to choose three ingredients and say what each one gives. Write the recipe.
flow.say: A one-year-old needs a lot from a small helping. Which three foods will you choose? What does each one give the child?
flow.kid: Choose a cereal, a pulse and a nut or seed. What does each give?

ask.q: Why must the mix have both a cereal and a pulse?
good: Together they give better protein.
Each fills the gap in the other's building units.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Health Mix for a One-Year-Old. You choose three ingredients and say what each gives.

flow.do: A grown-up roasts each ingredient separately on a low flame until it smells nutty. Cool them. Grind them together to a fine powder and sieve it.
flow.say: I will roast each one until it smells nutty, and then grind them. Why do you think we roast them first?
flow.kid: A grown-up roasts and grinds. Watch and smell. Why roast first?
flow.parent: Roasting dries the grains so the mix keeps. It also cooks them partly, so the porridge is easier to digest. Ragi takes about 5 minutes and groundnuts about 4.
flow.context: In this step of A Health Mix for a One-Year-Old a grown-up roasts and grinds your three ingredients.

flow.do: Stir 2 tablespoons of the mix into 1 cup of cold water until smooth. A grown-up cooks it on a low flame for 5 minutes, stirring all the time. Cool it and taste it.
flow.say: Mix the powder into cold water first, so it does not form lumps. I will cook it. Then you taste it and check it is smooth.
flow.kid: Stir the mix into cold water. A grown-up cooks it. Taste it. Is it smooth?
flow.context: In this step of A Health Mix for a One-Year-Old you cook your mix into a porridge and taste it.

flow.do: Check the porridge against each rule. Find the price of a packet baby cereal at a shop or online. Compare it with the rough cost of your mix. Ask what your child would change.
flow.say: Does your mix pass every rule? What does a packet baby cereal cost for the same weight? What would you change in your recipe?
flow.kid: Check each rule. Compare the cost with a packet. What would you change?
flow.parent: Mixes like this are given to young children by anganwadis in many states. In Kerala, women's groups make a mix of wheat, soya, chana and groundnut for them. Your child eats this porridge. Do not feed a new food to a real baby without the parents' say.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Health Mix for a One-Year-Old. You check your porridge against the rules and compare its cost with a packet.

items.p: What is a balanced diet?
opts: Enough of every nutrient for one person's body
As much food as a person can eat
The same plate for every person
items.why: A balanced diet gives one person enough of every nutrient, with water and fibre, and not too much of any. 'As much as you can eat' and 'the same for everyone' both ignore what one body needs.

items.p: Match each deficiency disease to the nutrient that is missing.
items.why: Each nutrient does its own job, so each lack shows in its own way: in the eyes, the gums, the bones, the blood, the neck or the nerves.

items.p: An illness caused by too little of one nutrient for a long time is called a ____ disease.
items.why: Deficiency means not having enough. Scurvy, rickets and goitre are deficiency diseases.

items.p: A person who always eats until they are full cannot have a deficiency disease.
items.why: False. Feeling full tells the body about energy and bulk. A person can be full of rice and still short of iron, iodine or vitamin A. This is hidden hunger.

items.p: Which pair of foods gives better protein together than either gives alone?
items.why: Rice is short of the building unit lysine, and dal is short of methionine. Each fills the other's gap. Sugar, ghee and tea add no protein.

items.p: Sort these nutrients. Is each one needed in grams, or in milligrams or less, each day?
items: protein
Grams
carbohydrate
Grams
fat
Grams
iron
Milligrams or less
iodine
Milligrams or less
vitamin C
Milligrams or less
items.why: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are fuel and building material, so the body needs grams of them. Vitamins and minerals do special jobs, and tiny amounts are enough.

items.p: Sunlight that comes through closed window glass makes vitamin D in the skin.
items.why: False. Glass blocks the rays that make vitamin D. The skin needs direct sunlight, with the Sun high in the sky.

items.p: Why is iodine added to salt, and not to sweets?
opts: Nearly everyone eats a little salt daily
items.why: Rich and poor eat salt every day in nearly the same small amount. So everyone gets enough iodine and nobody gets far too much.

items.p: The red substance in blood that carries oxygen and holds iron is called ____.
items.why: Each haemoglobin molecule holds four atoms of iron. With too little iron the body makes too little haemoglobin, and less oxygen is carried.

items.p: In the Dark Room Test, the dark book appeared only after several minutes. Explain why eyes need this time.
items.a: Bright light breaks down rhodopsin, the substance in the eye that catches dim light. In the dark the eye rebuilds it slowly from vitamin A. Dim things appear as more of it is rebuilt.
items.why: A strong answer says that something in the eye is used up by light and rebuilt in the dark. It names vitamin A as the material.

items.p: A child of 2 and a grandmother of 70 share one family pot. Write one change for each, with a reason.
items.a: For the child of 2: mash the food and leave out the chilli. Give small amounts five or six times a day, because the stomach is small. For the grandmother: softer food and a smaller helping, with curd, ragi or sesame, because she needs less energy and more calcium.
items.why: A strong answer gives a change and ties it to that person's body: a small stomach and fast growth, or weaker teeth and bones.

items.p: Draw a balanced plate for yourself for one meal. Label the food that gives energy, protein, iron, calcium and vitamin C.
items.a: A cereal or millet for energy. A pulse, egg, fish or curd for protein. Greens or a pulse for iron. Curd, milk or ragi for calcium. A fruit, tomato or lemon for vitamin C. One food may carry two labels.
items.why: A strong drawing uses foods the child really eats, and shows that one food can do more than one job.
items.art: An empty round steel plate with five blank label lines around it.

items.p: At a family meal, should every person get the same helping?

views.says: Yes. Equal helpings are fair. Nobody can complain that someone else got more.
No. A helping should match the body. A toddler, a girl of fourteen and a grandmother need different amounts.

views.who: A cook who feeds a large family
views.says: I start everyone with a fair helping. Then I watch who is still hungry and who leaves food, and I change the helpings.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about bodies. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason: a child of 2 needs about 85 kilocalories for each kilogram and a woman at a desk about 30. Another: equal helpings are simple and stop quarrels, but they leave growing children and hard workers short.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact about needs, such as growth, work, pregnancy or age. It treats the other view fairly.

items.p: Put these in order, from the largest amount a child needs each day to the smallest.
items: Iron
Protein
Iodine
Vitamin C
items.why: A child needs about 30 grams of protein and 50 milligrams of vitamin C. They need about 16 to 28 milligrams of iron and 100 micrograms of iodine. A milligram is a thousandth of a gram, and a microgram is a thousandth of a milligram.

items.p: A child sees well at noon but stumbles in a dim room. Which nutrient may be short?
items.why: The eye builds its dim-light substance from vitamin A. Trouble seeing at dusk, called night blindness, is the first sign of too little.

items.p: Why does a squeeze of lemon on kala chana help the body?
opts: Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron
Lemon adds a lot of protein
items.why: The iron in plant foods is hard to absorb. Vitamin C in the same meal changes the iron into a form that crosses the gut wall more easily.

items.p: Boiled cabbage water cleared the blue liquid in 2 teaspoons. Cold cabbage water took 7. What follows?
opts: More vitamin C moved into the boiled water
The cabbage held no vitamin C
items.why: Fewer teaspoons means more vitamin C in each teaspoon. Heat softened the cells of the leaf, so more of the vitamin leaked into the water.

items.p: A girl of 36 kilograms needs 2,060 kilocalories. A woman of 55 kilograms needs 1,660. Who needs more for each kilogram?
items.why: 2,060 divided by 36 is about 57. 1,660 divided by 55 is about 30. The girl is growing, so each kilogram of her body needs more.

items.p: Polishing rice until it is white removes most of its vitamin B1.
items.why: True. Vitamin B1 sits in the outer layers and the germ of the grain. Polishing takes these off as bran. This is why beriberi spread with machine-polished rice.

items.p: Taking extra vitamin A tablets every day makes healthy eyes see better and better.
items.why: False. Once the body has enough vitamin A, more does not help. Far too much is a poison that harms the liver and bones.

items.p: Three of these help the body get more iron from a meal. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Vitamin C from lemon and tomato helps iron cross the gut wall, and an iron kadai adds a little iron. Substances in tea hold on to iron, so less is absorbed.

items.p: Salt holds 15 micrograms of iodine in each gram. How many micrograms of iodine are in 6 grams of salt?
items.why: 6 grams hold 6 times 15, which is 90 micrograms.

items.p: Sort these signs. Does each belong to kwashiorkor or to marasmus?
items: swollen feet and face
Kwashiorkor
peeling skin
Kwashiorkor
very thin, with loose skin
Marasmus
no swelling
Marasmus
items.why: In kwashiorkor water gathers in the feet, legs and face, and the skin and hair change. In marasmus the child gets too little of everything and becomes very thin, with no swelling.

items.p: Match each kitchen habit to the reason it works.
pairs: The growing seed makes vitamin C
Cooking greens in little water with a lid
Less vitamin is lost to water
Each fills the other's protein gap
items.why: None of these habits costs much. Each one raises the nourishment the body gets from the same cheap food.

items.p: Explain how a person can be overweight and anaemic at the same time.
items.a: Fried snacks, sweets and sweet drinks give a lot of energy but very little iron. The extra energy is stored as body fat. The body still cannot make enough haemoglobin without iron.
items.why: A strong answer separates energy from micronutrients. Too much of one does not make up for too little of the other.

items.p: After the flash in the Dark Room Test, only the covered eye still saw the book. What does this show?
items.a: The light changed something inside the eye that it entered. The covered eye kept its dim-light substance, and the open eye lost it. So the change happens in each eye, and the room itself did not change.
items.why: A strong answer uses the two eyes as a comparison: same room, same moment, and only the light differed.

items.p: The sea holds iodine, and hill soils hold little. Explain why goitre was common in the Himalayas, and what changed that.
items.a: Rain washes iodine out of hill soils, so crops grown there hold little, and sea fish are far away. People's thyroid glands swelled as they tried to catch more iodine. Adding iodine to salt gave everyone enough.
items.why: A strong answer links the soil to the food and the food to the thyroid. It links the cure to a food that everyone eats.

items.p: Tablets or food: what is the best way to end anaemia in India?

views.says: Iron tablets work fast and cost little. I give them to pregnant women and schoolgirls, and I see their blood improve.

views.who: A grandmother who cooks for a family
views.says: Greens, ragi, chana and lemon carry iron along with many other nutrients. Food feeds the whole family every day.
People at risk need tablets now, in measured doses. But a country cannot live on tablets. Diets must change too.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For tablets: a pregnant woman needs more iron than food easily gives. For food: it carries many nutrients together, and too much iron in tablets is harmful. A strong answer may say both are needed for different people.
items.why: This is a real question that health planners argue about. A strong answer says who needs what, and why.

items.p: On an outline of a body, label where each of these shows: night blindness, goitre, rickets, scurvy.
a: Goitre: the front of the neck, where the thyroid gland sits
items.why: Each deficiency shows in the part of the body that depends most on the missing nutrient.
items.art: An outline of a child's body with four blank label lines pointing to the eyes, the neck, the mouth and the legs.

items.p: The substance in the eye that catches dim light, and is built from vitamin A, is called ____.
items.why: Rhodopsin fills the rod cells of the retina. Bright light breaks it down, and the eye rebuilds it in the dark.

items.p: A ship's doctor gave sick sailors the same meals, with a different addition for each pair. Why the same meals?
opts: So only the addition could explain a recovery
So the cook had less work
So the sailors would not quarrel
items.why: This was James Lind's test in 1747. Everything else was the same. So the quick recovery of the pair given oranges and lemons could only be due to the fruit.

items.p: In a test of iodised salt, some villages were given plain salt. Why?
opts: To compare with villages given iodised salt
items.why: Goitre might have fallen for some other reason, such as better roads or more food. Only a comparison group shows what the iodine itself did.

items.p: Which is the best evidence that tea with a meal reduces the iron absorbed?
opts: Less traced iron reached the blood with tea
Tea drinkers say they feel tired
Tea plants grow in iron-poor soil
items.why: Scientists gave meals holding iron atoms they could trace, and measured how much reached the blood. A measurement beats a guess from colour or from feelings.

items.p: A slow time in the Dark Room Test proves that a child is short of vitamin A.
items.why: False. The time depends mostly on how dark the room is and how bright the light was before. Age matters too. Only a doctor can tell whether vitamin A is short.

items.p: In north India in December, a pencil's shadow can stay longer than the pencil all day.
items.why: True. In winter the Sun stays low in the northern sky all day. Shadows stay long, and skin makes little vitamin D.

items.p: RICE holds 2 rajma and 6 chana. DAL holds 6 and 2. How many bricks from 3 RICE and 1 DAL?
items.why: Rajma: 3 times 2, plus 6, is 12. Chana: 3 times 6, plus 2, is 20. A brick needs one of each, so the 12 rajma set the limit. Eight chana are left over.

items.p: Put these steps in order, from a leaf to seeing in dim light.
items: The eye builds rhodopsin from vitamin A
A plant makes carotene
The gut wall splits carotene into vitamin A
Rhodopsin catches dim light
A person eats the leaf
Blood carries vitamin A to the eye
a: The gut wall splits carotene into vitamin A
Blood carries vitamin A to the eye
The eye builds rhodopsin from vitamin A
items.why: The carotene is made by the plant. The body changes it in two places: the gut wall makes vitamin A, and the eye builds rhodopsin.

items.p: Adding a nutrient to a common food, so that everyone who eats it gets enough, is called ____.
items.why: Iodised salt is the best-known fortified food. Some oil and milk are fortified with vitamins A and D.

items.p: Many people believe spinach is the best food for iron. What would you measure to check this?
items.a: Measure how much iron from the food reaches the blood. Compare it with other foods such as bajra, chana or egg. The iron a food holds and the iron the body absorbs are different amounts.
items.why: A strong answer sees that 'holds iron' and 'gives the body iron' are two claims. The second needs a measurement in a person.

items.p: Design a fair test of this question: does a lid on the vessel save vitamin C when cabbage is boiled?
items.a: Boil two equal cups of cabbage in equal water for the same time, one with a lid and one without. Top up both waters to the same amount and cool them. Test each with the blue liquid and count the teaspoons. Repeat once.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the lid and keeps the cabbage, water and time the same. It says what will be counted.

items.p: Villages lower down a stream had more goitre. What test could tell a germ in the water from a missing nutrient?
items.a: Give some villages iodine and leave their water unchanged. If goitre falls there and not in the other villages, the cause was the missing iodine. Boiling the water in some villages would test the germ idea.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing at a time and keeps a comparison group. The same pattern can have two explanations, and only a test separates them.

items.p: India grows enough grain for everyone, yet many people are anaemic. Give two reasons from this unit.
items.a: Grain gives energy but little iron that the body can absorb. Pulses, greens and millets cost more or are grown less than before. Tea with meals reduces the iron absorbed. In many families women and girls eat last and least.
items.why: A strong answer separates enough energy from enough micronutrients, and gives reasons about food, cost or habits.

items.p: From the 1960s India grew far more wheat and rice. Was that a full success?

views.says: My harvest grew several times over. India stopped waiting for ships of grain from abroad. Famines ended.
Energy became cheap, but iron, protein and vitamins did not. Hidden hunger stayed, because grain alone is not a balanced diet.
Ragi and jowar need little water and hold more calcium and iron. Yet prices and ration shops favoured rice and wheat, so fewer people grew millets.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views with a fact from this unit.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The farmer is right that famine ended. The scientist is right that more than half of India's women are still anaemic. The millet farmer is right that ragi has about three times the calcium of milk.
items.why: All three speakers describe something true. A strong answer weighs ending famine against ending hidden hunger.

items.p: Draw one rod cell of the eye twice: after bright light, and after 20 minutes of dark. Show the rhodopsin.
items.a: After bright light: a long thin cell with almost no dots of rhodopsin. After 20 minutes of dark: the same cell packed with dots. An arrow shows vitamin A arriving in the blood to build them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same cell in two states, and shows where the material for rebuilding comes from.

quiz.p: Which meal is the most balanced for a child of ten?

White rice with ghee and sugar
Chips, biscuits and a sweet drink
Three kinds of fruit and nothing else
quiz.why: The first meal has a millet, a pulse, a green vegetable, curd and a vitamin C fruit. The others each leave out protein, iron or energy.

quiz.p: A person's gums bleed and small wounds do not heal. Which nutrient is most likely missing?
quiz.why: Vitamin C helps build collagen, the strong threads in gums, skin and blood vessels. Without it they weaken. The disease is scurvy.

quiz.p: Which cheap food helps most to prevent night blindness?
quiz.why: Drumstick leaves are rich in carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A. Rice, sugar and tea hold almost none.

opts: Lacking a vitamin or mineral while feeling full
Eating too fast to taste the food
quiz.why: Fullness reports energy and bulk. A person can feel full and still be short of iron, iodine or vitamin A.

quiz.p: Who needs the most energy for each kilogram of body weight?
opts: A woman who works at a desk
A man who works at a desk
quiz.why: A child of 2 needs about 85 kilocalories for each kilogram, because they are growing fast. A grown-up at a desk needs about 30.

quiz.p: Why does a breastfeeding mother need extra food?
opts: She makes milk that feeds a growing baby
quiz.why: She makes about 750 millilitres of milk a day. Everything in it comes from her own food and body, and it costs her about 600 kilocalories.

quiz.p: Why should the water from boiled vegetables go into the dish?
opts: It holds most of the protein
It makes the dish cook faster
quiz.why: Vitamin C and the B vitamins dissolve in water. Pouring the water away throws them out. Rasam, sambar and kootu keep it.

quiz.p: Why do rice and dal together give better protein than rice alone?
opts: Each supplies a building unit the other lacks
Rice has no protein at all
quiz.why: Rice is short of lysine and dal is short of methionine. The body builds with complete sets, so together they build more.

quiz.p: Why are iron tablets taken only on the advice of a health worker?
quiz.why: The body needs a measured amount. A large dose of iron can poison a child. Health workers give the dose that suits the person.

quiz.p: In a fair test of two ways of cooking cabbage, what must stay the same?
opts: The cabbage, the water and the time
Only the colour of the vessel
Nothing needs to stay the same
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing. If the amount of cabbage, the water and the time are equal, any difference comes from the cooking method.

quiz.p: Goitre fell only in villages that were given iodised salt. What did that show?
opts: Too little iodine was the main cause
Goitre spreads from person to person
quiz.why: The villages differed in one thing, the iodine in their salt. So the fall in goitre was due to iodine. Plain salt did not cause goitre. It only failed to prevent it.

applications: Iodised salt carries iodine to nearly every home in India. Since it spread, goitre has become rare in places where it was once common.
Health workers put vitamin A drops in the mouths of young children twice a year. The drops protect their eyes and help them fight infections.
Pregnant women and schoolchildren are given iron and folic acid tablets at health centres and schools, to prevent anaemia.

School lunches in India are planned by nutrition rules: a cereal, a pulse, vegetables and oil. Tamil Nadu has served free school lunches for decades, and many schools add eggs.
Plant breeders have bred bajra with more iron and wheat with more zinc. Farmers grow them like any other variety.
Hospitals plan a separate diet for each patient: soft food after an operation, extra protein for healing, and less salt for a weak heart.

open_questions.why_open: Too little protein does not explain why one child gets it and another on the same food does not. Gut microbes, infections and missing protective nutrients are all being studied.

open_questions.q: Why are so many people in sunny India short of vitamin D?
open_questions.why_open: Indoor life, covered skin, air pollution and darker skin may each play a part. Nobody knows how much each matters, and experts disagree about what level counts as too low.

open_questions.q: How much of each nutrient does one particular person need?
open_questions.why_open: The numbers in tables are averages with a safety margin. Bodies, genes and gut microbes differ, and scientists are only beginning to measure by how much.

open_questions.q: Do vitamin tablets help people who already eat a varied diet?
open_questions.why_open: Large studies have mostly found little benefit for well-fed adults. Scientists still argue about which groups gain from them.

open_questions.q: Can crops bred or changed to hold more vitamins and minerals end hidden hunger?
open_questions.why_open: Such crops help in trials. Whether enough farmers grow them and enough families eat them is still being tested. People also disagree about some of the methods.
