maths.problem: In the Dark Room Test, the white towel appeared after 40 seconds and the dark book after 380 seconds. How many times as long did the dark book take?
maths.answer: 9 and a half times as long.
maths.explain: 380 divided by 40 is 9.5. So the dark book took nine and a half times as long to appear as the white towel.
maths.context: In the Dark Room Test you sit in a dark room after bright light. You time how long each thing takes to appear. These are made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other shows how much harder a dark thing is to see than a pale one.

maths.problem: A child of 2 weighs 13 kilograms and needs 1,110 kilocalories a day. A woman weighs 55 kilograms and needs 1,660. Who needs more for each kilogram, and about how many times as much?
maths.answer: The child: about 85 against about 30, which is nearly 3 times as much.
maths.explain: 1,110 divided by 13 is about 85. 1,660 divided by 55 is about 30. 85 divided by 30 is about 2.8. So for each kilogram, the child needs nearly 3 times as much.
maths.context: In Seven People, One Pot you use a table of what different people need in a day. These figures are from that table.
maths.why_maths: Total amounts hide the pattern. Dividing by body weight shows that growing bodies need the most for their size.

maths.problem: A salt packet holds 30 micrograms of iodine in each gram. A child needs 100 micrograms a day. How many grams of this salt hold a day's iodine?
maths.answer: About 3 grams, which is a little more than half a level teaspoon.
maths.explain: 100 divided by 30 is about 3.3. So about 3 grams of salt hold 100 micrograms of iodine. A level teaspoon of salt is about 5 to 6 grams.
maths.context: In Find What Was Added you read how much iodine a salt packet holds. This problem uses a common figure from such packets.
maths.why_maths: The sum shows that ordinary salting is enough, so nobody needs to eat extra salt for iodine.

maths.problem: Groundnuts cost 14 rupees for 100 grams and hold 24 grams of protein. Paneer costs 40 rupees for 100 grams and holds 19 grams. How much protein does 10 rupees buy in each?
maths.answer: About 17 grams in groundnuts, and about 5 grams in paneer.
maths.explain: Groundnuts: 24 divided by 14 is about 1.7 grams for each rupee, so 10 rupees buy about 17 grams. Paneer: 19 divided by 40 is about 0.5 grams for each rupee, so 10 rupees buy about 5 grams.
maths.context: In Protein for Ten Rupees you work out how much protein ten rupees buys in different foods. These prices are made up.
maths.why_maths: A price alone does not show value. Dividing protein by price lets you compare two very different foods fairly.

maths.problem: A RICE slip holds 2 rajma and 6 chana. A DAL slip holds 6 rajma and 2 chana. A brick needs one of each. Which builds more bricks: 4 RICE slips, or 3 RICE slips and 1 DAL slip?
maths.explain: 4 RICE slips hold 8 rajma and 24 chana, so they build 8 bricks. 3 RICE and 1 DAL hold 12 rajma and 20 chana, so they build 12 bricks. Swapping one slip in four adds half as many bricks again.
maths.context: In Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks, rajma and chana stand for two building units of protein. A brick of body protein needs one of each.
maths.why_maths: Counting the scarcer unit shows why a little dal with a lot of rice raises what the body can build.

maths.problem: In the Cooking Water Test, boiled cabbage water cleared the blue liquid in 2 teaspoons. Cold cabbage water took 7. Plain water did not clear it in 10. Which liquid held the most vitamin C in each teaspoon? Explain why plain water was tested at all.
maths.answer: The boiled cabbage water held the most. Plain water was the comparison.
maths.explain: Fewer teaspoons means more vitamin C in each one, so 2 teaspoons beats 7. Plain water shows that simply adding liquid does not clear the blue. Without it, nobody could be sure the cabbage did anything.
maths.context: In the Cooking Water Test you add liquids to a blue test liquid, one teaspoon at a time. You count until the blue is gone. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Here a smaller number means more vitamin. Reading the numbers the right way round is part of reading data.

maths.problem: In the Short Shadow Test, a pencil stood 18 centimetres tall. The shadows were 40, 14, 4 and 30 centimetres long at 8, 10, 12 and 4 o'clock. At which times was the shadow shorter than the pencil? What fraction of the pencil's height was the noon shadow?
maths.answer: At 10 and at 12. The noon shadow was two ninths of the pencil's height.
maths.explain: 14 and 4 are less than 18, and 40 and 30 are more. The noon shadow is 4 out of 18. Divide both by 2 to get 2 out of 9.
maths.context: In the Short Shadow Test you measure the shadow of an upright pencil at four times of day. These are made-up lengths.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each shadow with the pencil turns four lengths into a simple answer: when is the Sun high?

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how doctors found the cause of goitre, the swelling of the neck. It took about a hundred years and tests on three continents.
how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, many people in the Himalayas lived with goitre, a swelling at the front of the neck. From 1902 a British army doctor, Robert McCarrison, studied goitre in Gilgit. Villages lower down a water channel had more goitre than villages higher up. So he decided that dirty water carried something, perhaps a germ, that caused goitre. Half a century earlier, a French pharmacist and botanist named Adolphe Chatin had measured iodine in water and plants. He found less iodine in places where goitre was common. Many doctors doubted him. The test began about 1917 in Akron, a town in the United States. David Marine and O. P. Kimball gave about two thousand schoolgirls small doses of iodine. Only five of them developed goitre. Among the girls who took no iodine, nearly five hundred did. In 1956 Dr V. Ramalingaswami and his team began a larger test in the Kangra valley, now part of Himachal Pradesh. Some villages got salt with iodine added, and others got plain salt. After about five or six years, goitre had fallen by about half or more where the salt was iodised. It had not fallen where the salt was plain. In 1962 India began a national programme to iodise salt.
how_we_found_out.who: Adolphe Chatin in France, Robert McCarrison in Gilgit, David Marine and O. P. Kimball in the United States, and V. Ramalingaswami and S. S. Sooch in the Kangra valley
how_we_found_out.when: Chatin published his iodine measurements from 1850. McCarrison worked in Gilgit from 1902. Marine and Kimball's test began about 1917. The Kangra valley study began in 1956, and India's salt programme in 1962.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That goitre is caused by a germ in dirty water. Marine and Kimball showed that a small dose of iodine prevented goitre in schoolgirls. The Kangra valley study showed that iodine in salt did the same for whole villages.
how_we_found_out.art: A doctor in a hill village in the 1950s weighing out salt from a sack marked with a painted sign, while women with cloth bags wait in a line.

roots.context: In this unit you timed your eyes in a dark room. You learned that vitamin A lets them see in dim light. Here we ask where that vitamin A came from, and what that says about you.

deep_truth.truth: In the Dark Room Test, the dark book showed up only after several minutes. In that time, your eyes rebuilt a light-catching substance from vitamin A. All vitamin A begins as carotene, an orange colour that plants and algae make. So your eyes see in dim light with a colour that a plant made.
deep_truth.habit: We think of seeing as something our eyes do by themselves. We think of food as fuel that is burned and gone. Some food is never burned. Its molecules become working parts of the body, and the body has no other way to get them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dark Room Test, sight in dim light comes back slowly, because the eye must rebuild rhodopsin. People short of vitamin A stay blind in dim light. Animals cannot make vitamin A from nothing. They make it from the carotene of plants and algae, or get it from another animal who did.

three.who_am_i: You are built partly from things that other living beings made for their own lives. The substance that lets you see at dusk began as a colour in a leaf or a fruit.
three.what_is_life: No living being makes everything they need. Plants make carotene and vitamin C, bacteria make vitamin B12, and your skin makes vitamin D with the Sun. Every body depends on what other bodies make.
three.what_is_this_world: Iodine comes originally from the sea, and iodised salt carries a little of it to your food. Your thyroid needs only a few atoms of iodine to work. So very small amounts of something can do very large jobs inside you.

roots.thread: A drumstick leaf makes carotene, which helps the leaf catch sunlight and protects the leaf from too much of it. You eat the leaf. Your gut wall splits each carotene molecule into vitamin A. Your eye joins the vitamin A to a protein, and the new substance catches light again, this time for you. Many sages taught that all beings live by one another. The science here shows one exact case of it. A substance that worked with light in a plant goes on working with light in your eye.

teachings.teaching: From food all beings are born. By food they live, and into food they return at the end.
teachings.link: The verse says that every living body is made from other living bodies. Vitamin A is a small, exact example. Animals do not make vitamin A from nothing, so the vitamin passes from plant to animal to animal. The Upanishad says this as an insight about all life, which science does not test.

teachings.teaching: A body needs no medicine if a person eats only after the last meal is digested. Eat in the measure that suits your body.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar ties health to a measure of food that fits one body. This unit shows that the measure differs: a girl of ten, a pregnant woman and a grandmother each need a different plate. The couplets give advice. They do not name nutrients.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, 'interbeing', in The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the forest there. Nothing exists by itself alone.
teachings.link: Look at your own eye in the same way. The substance that catches dim light in it began in a leaf or a fruit. This is a way of looking, and the facts about vitamin A stand without it.

science.text: Animals cannot make vitamin A from nothing. It starts as carotene made by plants, algae and some microbes, and passes along food chains.
Humans, other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs and some bats cannot make vitamin C, because one gene no longer works. Most other animals make their own.
The microbes in a person's gut may change how much of some nutrients that person needs. Scientists are still measuring how much.

other_view.view: Carotene is a molecule and nothing more. Once your gut wall has split it and your eye has built it into rhodopsin, it is fully yours. Nothing of the plant remains. Saying that you see with a plant's colour only describes where some atoms were last week.

practice.title: Watching the room come back
practice.say: Switch off the light at night and sit still. At first the room is black. Breathe slowly and keep your eyes open. Notice the first thing that appears, and then the next. Your eyes are rebuilding their light-catching substance now. Think of the last orange or green food you ate. Some of that food is at work in your eyes.
practice.kid: Switch off the light. Sit still and breathe slowly. Watch what appears first. Your eyes are rebuilding. Think of a carrot or a green leaf you ate.

ask: In the Dark Room Test, your eyes rebuilt their light-catching substance from vitamin A. That vitamin A began in a plant. Is the substance yours or the plant's?
A goat makes her own vitamin C, and you must get yours from fruit and leaves. What does your body gain or lose by depending on plants?

The iodine you need in a whole day weighs about the same as a speck of chalk dust the size of a full stop. That is a very small amount, yet your body falls ill without it. What else that is very small might be doing large jobs inside you?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. The Dark Room Test (core) needs a room that is nearly dark and a grown-up outside the door. Times depend mostly on how dark the room is, so the steps say how to make it darker or lighter. A slow time does not mean a child lacks vitamin A. The Cooking Water Test (core) needs povidone-iodine or tincture of iodine, rice water and cabbage. The blue liquid must be pale, and the cooking water must be cooled first. Boiled cabbage water should clear the blue in a few teaspoons. Cold cabbage water should take many more, or not clear it. Plain water never clears it. The count is a rough measure, because a few other substances in cabbage also clear iodine. The Short Shadow Test needs a spot with direct sunlight and a sunny day. In north India in winter the shadow may never be shorter than the pencil. The step says that this is a real result. Four activities need only kitchen things, paper and your own shop prices. They are One Day's Needs, Seven People, One Pot, Protein for Ten Rupees, and Rice Bricks and Dal Bricks. In Fill the Plate, every person card was checked: each can be balanced within the card limit, and the pregnant woman's plate is the hardest. The Health Mix challenge needs a mixer and a grown-up at the stove, and the child eats the porridge. No part needs a garden or an animal. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against the ICMR-NIN 2020 tables, the Indian Food Composition Tables 2017 and published papers: daily needs and food protein figures were corrected. The Akron and Kangra goitre figures, the dates and the Lind result were softened where sources differ. The short-shadow rule is a rule of thumb. The amounts in One Day's Needs are rough.
